#7908. What Makes a Lucky Dog? | Heroes of the Pet World

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

Maybe it is having a family that loves them. Maybe it is a warm bed, a full bowl, and a safe place to sleep. Or maybe luck is something a little more fundamental: having people who see you as an individual and take the time to understand what you need.

At Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption Center near Lake Chapala, Mexico, the dogs may still be waiting for permanent homes, but in the meantime, they are surrounded by caring people who show up for them day after day.

At Lucky Dog, everyone has a unique way to help and collaborate.

Some volunteers walk dogs. Others train them, clean their enclosures, help with fundraising, or coordinate veterinary care. Some foster dogs in their homes. Others help with the less visible work that keeps the center running.

When I visited Lucky Dog, I arrived with Mark and Nancy. Mark helped build the Thursday volunteer group, bringing together people who wanted to help in different ways.

âI've gotten to know a lot of people who want to help, and somehow Thursday became our day. We have our group, and everybody has something they can do. You don't have to do everything. You just have to show up and help with what you can.â

Mark has an injured knee, and at the moment, he cannot walk the long distances over cobblestone roads around the center, but he and Nancy have their own important role. They bring chairs into the enclosures and spend about 20 minutes with the dogs, offering pats, treats, kind words, and ear scratches. The dogs happily settle in beside them.

Different volunteer groups cover each day of the week. Some take dogs for walks, while others help with training, cleaning, maintenance, administration, or fundraising.

That Thursday, each person simply did what they came to do. For the dogs, every part of that effort is what makes them feel lucky.

During the day, the dogs stay in pairs in larger enclosures. They are taken out for long walks or playtime in the larger garden areas around the center. In the mornings and evenings, Valentin, one of only two paid workers at the rescue, moves the dogs between their daytime and nighttime enclosures and feeds them breakfast and dinner. During the day, volunteers help with walks, playtime, training, and puppy lunchtime.

At night, the dogs return to smaller individual enclosures.

When a dog needs medical attention, a veterinarian comes to the center to examine and treat them. Volunteers then follow the veterinarian's instructions and continue treatment.

From Valentin's morning and evening routine to the volunteers who walk, train, feed, and care for the dogs, many people contribute to a Lucky Dog's day.

The roots of today's Lucky Dog Rescue go back to 2001, when Geoffrey Kaye and Lourdes Avila started an animal shelter in Riberas del Pilar. When the shelter closed in 2012, the commitment to helping the area's dogs continued. Volunteers regrouped with veterinarian Dr. Antonio Ladron, and in December 2012, Lucky Dog Rescue and Adoption opened its doors.

Since then, the center has continued caring for abandoned and abused dogs while helping prepare them for permanent homes.

In 2025, Lucky Dog took in 23 dogs and placed 23 through adoption or transfer. Approximately 35 new volunteers joined, with around 30 committing to weekly shifts. The center's intended capacity is 22 dogs, yet its average monthly census was close to 30 during the year.

Those numbers give you some idea of the work happening behind every individual dog.

Spicy is dog-reactive and needs to be housed separately from other dogs. Mark has developed a close relationship with her, and she has a very clear opinion about where his attention should go.

âSpicy loves me, and she is not happy when she sees me go into a different enclosure to pet another dog,â Mark said. âI have to do it in a way that I hide from her so she canât see or she won't stop barking.â

It is a sweet story, but it also shows why understanding each dog's personality matters.

Hope Procops, who works as a groundskeeper and guard at Lucky Dog, understands how important volunteers are to organizations like this. Itâs not just about the day-to-day tasks. Itâs about looking after the dogs in their care and preparing them for life beyond the shelter. She says the goal of Lucky Dog Rescue is âto ensure all the dogs in our care are kept healthy, loved, socialized, and given the best chance to find their forever homes.â

Camille Short is in charge of training volunteers and dogs at Lucky Dog. Her approach goes beyond teaching basic commands. The goal is to help dogs develop skills that can help them succeed in a home.

Three young siblings, Sasha, Stephanie, and Sergio, were already showing how quickly puppies can learn. They knew how to sit and lie down on command, and were learning to walk with their harnesses. They were highly motivated by treats and, judging by the puppy kisses, equally enthusiastic about people.

Two of the puppies, Stephanie and Sergio, have already been chosen by families; their adoption papers are signed and ready. Sasha remains available for adoption.

As for Spicy, she arrived at Lucky Dog in 2022 and has been waiting for her new home ever since. Initially anxious and mistrustful, she has come a long way with the daily attention and interactions she receives from volunteers. Now, Spicy is looking for a confident new best friend.

âEverything nice with a little bit of spice,â says Camille of Spicy. âShe loves people and attention but is selective about her four-legged friends.â

Some dogs find their people quickly. Others need more time, medical care, or someone who understands their particular personality. Until then, their days continue with walks, play, veterinary care, clean enclosures, treats, kind words, and volunteers who take the time to understand them.

Vice President of Lucky Dog Rescue, Darryl Painter, describes the mission as:

âImproving animal welfare in Lake Chapala via rescue, adoption, community, and fostering.â

The sense of community was tangible during my visit, but perhaps what stayed with me most was how much we humans and dogs have in common. We are all sentient beings, and in our own ways, we all need to be acknowledged, accepted for who we are, and given the opportunity to love and be loved.

At Lucky Dog, those needs are met in many different ways. A walk, a clean enclosure, a treat, a kind word, or simply having someone take the time to know an individual dog.

Not just having people who care for them, but having people who take the time to know them.

And that is something anyone can do. Whether it is volunteering, fostering, sponsoring, or simply offering time and attention, there is a way to help.

Someone opens an enclosure.Someone picks up a leash.Someone brings a treat.

And perhapsâ¦that is what makes these dogs lucky.

#7906. What’s up, Butt? What a Cat’s Trying to Say With Their Derrière in the Air

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

A female cat suddenly raising her hindquarters into the air, her tail swishing suggestively, can seem like a strange new behavior. In an unspayed female, though, it's often one of the clearest signs that she's gone into heat.

Heat, more correctly called âestrusâ, is a normal part of a cat's reproductive cycle, but it can bring several noticeable changes in behavior. Unspayed cats typically experience their first heat or season between six and nine months old, although some can start even earlier. After that first season, she will continue to come into heat roughly every 21 days, but during months with longer daylight hours, the cycle can repeat every two to three weeks.

As âlong-dayâ breeders, the female reproductive cycle of cats tends to be linked to warmer seasons when daylight hours are longer. However, depending on the climate and location, they can continue to cycle throughout the year.

Knowing what to look for can make the sudden change in behavior much easier to understand.

The insistent and attention-grabbing raising of the butt is certainly one of the hallmarks of a cat in estrus, but, like with so many feline behaviors, context is key. Here are some classic signs that are commonly â but not exclusively â displayed by a cat in heat.

The most recognizable behavior is the one that often gets the most attention. A female cat may raise her hindquarters and move her tail off to one side, a posture sometimes described as âpresentingâ.

This is a way for a female to signal to males that she's receptive to mating.

However, the posture by itself doesn't necessarily mean a cat is in heat, and many spayed females, and even male cats, will raise their hindquarters when being petted or while stretching their front legs. It's therefore more useful when considered alongside the other signs of heat.

A raised bum and attentive behavior from a spayed/neutered cat is often a sign of trust and affection.

A cat in heat can become considerably more vocal. The sounds can be loud and intense, and some owners may even mistake the vocalizing for a sign that their cat is in pain.

On its own, though, this behavior isn't usually cause for alarm in a cat that is otherwise showing the typical signs of heat. The vocalizing is part of the way a female calls for a mate.

Frequent vocalizing can have other causes, including illness or pain, so a cat showing additional signs that something isn't right should be checked by a vet.

Rolling around on the floor is hardly unusual for a cat. Cats of either sex may roll around while playing, seeking attention, or scratching an itch.

During heat, however, a female may do it more frequently as part of the behavioral changes that come with her reproductive cycle.

Like raising the hindquarters, rolling isn't enough to confirm that a cat is in heat on its own. It becomes more meaningful when it appears alongside several of the other signs.

Some cats become noticeably more affectionate when they're in heat. They may seek out attention more often, stay close to their owners, or generally seem more interested in interaction than usual.

There are plenty of other reasons a cat might become more affectionate. A cat could be looking for warmth in cold weather or seeking extra attention after being separated from an owner.

That makes increased affection more useful as part of a pattern rather than as a standalone sign.

Urine spraying is more commonly associated with unneutered male cats, but did you know that females can spray too? During heat, the scent is thought to help attract potential mates.

At the same time, urinating outside the litter box can have many other explanations. Litter box problems, behavioral issues, and medical complications can all cause changes in bathroom habits.

If a cat starts consistently going outside the litter box, it's worth discussing with a vet rather than assuming the behavior is simply related to heat.

A female cat in heat may become more determined to get outside. Scratching at doors or windows can be part of that behavior, particularly when a cat is trying to find a mate.

Keeping her indoors is especially important during this period. An unspayed female that gets outside has a risk of becoming pregnant, as well as facing the usual dangers associated with roaming, including traffic, animal attacks, and getting lost.

Responsible pet ownership means spaying or neutering your cat. By removing the ovaries and uterus, spaying stops the reproductive cycle permanently, preventing unwanted litters, reducing the risk of uterine infections, and meaningfully lowering the risk of mammary cancer. It also reduces the risks of cats escaping, fighting, and being hit by a car.

There are no health or behavioral advantages to allowing your female cat to have a litter, so veterinary advice is to spay and neuter most cats by 6 months.

Until then, recognizing the signs of heat can make a sudden change in behavior much less confusing. A female cat raising her hindquarters, becoming unusually vocal, rolling around, seeking extra attention, spraying, or trying to get outside may simply be responding to a normal part of her reproductive cycle.

Of course, it may simply be a catâs way of signalling trust and affection!

The season may be winding down but there’s plenty you can do now to protect those tubers so your dahlias come back stronger next summer. These 5 secrets unlock your best blooms ever

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first fall frosts bring a dramatic and abrupt curtain call to flower borders. And for any dahlias that might have been bursting with dinner-plate blooms just days earlier, it can come as a bit of a shock when freezing temperatures leave them limp and shriveled. For new dahlia growers, this sudden collapse can be devastating. Yet while the stems and leaves may be wilting and the flowers may be done, the tubers remain very much alive and capable of producing decades of future blooms.

So take heart, because you can enjoy those gorgeous displays again, as long as you take the right steps now. The days following first frosts are critical if these tubers are to push new growth out next year. These Mexican and Central American natives need care in order to see out the next few months. If these tubers are subjected to hard-frozen subsoil or waterlogged winter mud, they might easily rot and perish.

To keep your favorite cultivars thriving year after year, you need to decide how to overwinter dahlias, either by lifting the tubers for indoor storage or by applying the right protection and insulation in milder regions. The right approach depends on your regional hardiness zone, local soil drainage, and weather. While it might be a little daunting at first, getting your dahlias ready for winter is a relatively simple process. Whether you lift or leave in the ground, here’s how to prime your dahlias for winter.

Timing is key if you want your dahlia tubers to survive winter, and it’s vital to pay heed to your USDA hardiness zone to help your dahlia tubers to survive winter. Never dig your dahlias before the initial frost. That frost sends a biochemical signal through the plant, letting it know that the growing season has ended. In response, the plant channels its remaining energy down into the ground, plumping up the tubers in preparation for dormancy. So allowing the blackened stems to rest untouched for a week or so after this frost ensures the tubers reach peak maturity.

Your overwintering choices will depend on where you live. If you are in zones 6 and colder, it’s best to lift tubers every fall. Winter ground freezes in these latitudes can be lethal for unprotected tubers. Zone 7 gardens are borderline: lifting is still advised, but tubers in sandy, well-draining soil can survive beneath heavy insulation. In mild southern and coastal regions (zones 8-11), many dahlia varieties can remain safely in the ground, provided winter soil drains freely and the tubers have some protection.

You don’t have to remove the tubers right after the first frost. Let the foliage die back naturally. Any green foliage is still collecting energy to store in the tubers. You don’t want to disrupt that process prematurely. However, if you are in a very cold climate where the ground is going to freeze before the foliage has died, don’t wait. Keep an eye on the weather forecast to decide when to dig and lift your tubers. The goal is to let them mature without freezing them. In warmer climates, you have more flexibility.

Before you start, check the soil with a soil meter like the Raintrip 4-in-1 Soil Meter from Amazon. This will help you determine when the ground is nearing that freezing threshold ahead of lifting or mulching. Dahlia type and variety matter, too. Massive dinner plate varieties (such as Café au Lait) produce heavy tuber clumps that require longer drying times, whereas compact varieties (like the Gallery series) form tight root balls that dry quickly. Whichever area and variety you have, these steps will help you to ensure your dahlias return with a bang next summer…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The first step is to cut back stems and foliage. Once the foliage has blackened and you have allowed the root system a week to absorb its final starches, you’re ready. Using sharp bypass pruners, sever the main stalks down to 4-6 inches (10-15cm). If you are after a pair of bypass pruners, the Corona BP Dual Link Bypass Pruners from Amazon are perfect for slicing through the thick stalks in a single pass without crushing vital tissue.

Leaving short, sturdy stems is vital, as it gives you a safe gripping point for lifting the heavy tuber clusters and reduces pressure on delicate tuber necks. You can also use them to attach identifying labels. Just make sure that you cut the stalks just before lifting. Dahlia stalks are hollow, so if you cut stems down and leave them through days of heavy rain, water will pool around the tuber and trigger rot. Cut on a dry morning and plan to lift tubers the same day to keep water from causing problems.

Now, you’re ready to lift your tubers, but do it slowly and carefully. The tuberous roots and the narrow neck that connects them to the crown can break easily. If these necks snap, twist, or crack during digging, the tuber becomes useless. Use a garden fork to dig several inches around the plant. Get under the roots with the fork, inserting the tines 10-12 inches (25-30cm) away from the main stem. Rock the fork handle backward to loosen the soil, working in a full circle around the plant.

Gently lift the clump, using the shortened stems to help, but don’t yank hard on the stalk. Once lifted, gently shake away loose clods of earth. Inspect the roots, and snip away any soft, mushy, or damaged tubers. However, resist dividing the tubers now. Those cuts can leave them vulnerable to rot or infections in winter storage. You can add a little sulfur power such as Bonide Sulfur Plant Fungicide Dust from Walmart to stems to prevent storage rots. Alternatively, dust stem cuts with a little cinnamon.

Your tubers will need a little time to dry before being packed away. Place them upside down on slatted wooden trays, wire screens, or newspaper in a shaded, frost-free, well-ventilated space at 55-65°F (13-18°C). Let the clumps dry for 2-3 days until the skin feels dry and leathery. But don’t leave them so long that the tubers begin to wrinkle or shrivel.

Pack the dry tubers in breathable containers, such as cardboard boxes, wooden apple crates, or plastic storage totes with the lids cracked open. Nestle the tubers in a sterile, moisture-buffering medium, such as dry vermiculite, horticultural perlite, coarse wood shavings, or peat-free coir. You can buy Miracle-Gro Perlite from The Home Depot to help cushion dormant tubers while absorbing excess humidity to prevent winter mold. Make sure individual tubers do not touch.

Move your container into a dark, unheated room, such as a cellar, basement corner, or frost-free garage. Make sure it holds steady at 40-50°F (4-10°C). Stored tubers need a balance of moisture and dryness. Check on the tubers a few times over winter. If they are too moist, repack in drier material. If too dry, give them a light spritz of water.

If you are in zones 8-11 (or a sheltered microclimate in zone 7), you can overwinter your dahlia tubers in the ground. However, success depends on 3 factors: mild winters, excellent winter soil drainage, and insulation. Heavy clay soil that stays saturated in winter will rot tubers in the ground, regardless of ambient air warmth. Wait for the first frost to blacken the leaves, then cut the stalks down to 2-3 inches (5-8cm). Immediately cap the hollow stem ends with small inverted plastic cups, foil wraps, or a dab of horticultural wax to prevent rain from channeling into the crowns.

After cutting back dead stems, spread a generous 4-6-inch (10-15cm) blanket of loose, organic mulch over the surface. Try team favorite Back to the Roots Organic Premium Mulch from Amazon for a lush bark mulch that insulates from freeze-thaw cycles and suppresses weeds. You can also use clean agricultural straw or chopped dry leaves for protection against cold snaps, while helping to maintain healthy soil aeration.

Container-grown dahlias are vulnerable to freeze-thaw shocks. Left on an exposed patio, tubers can turn to ice in hours, while ceramic and terracotta planters are prone to cracking. It’s wise to move the container to a sheltered location for winter. Just be sure the soil will stay dry and the storage area won’t freeze. Once frost kills foliage, cut the stalks back to 4 inches (10cm), cease watering, and allow the potting mix to dry out. In colder regions, move the pot to an unheated garage, shed, or basement where temperatures are 35-45°F (2-7°C). If indoor space is unavailable in borderline zones, cluster containers tightly against a sheltered, south-facing foundation wall.

Wrap the containers in heavy layers of burlap or thermal bubble wrap, and mound loose straw over the top of the soil as a light mulch layer. Sta-Green Burlap Blankets from Lowe’s are a great breathable option for insulating grouped containers against winter winds and chills. Alternatively, you can lift and store tubers, just as with in-ground dahlias. Unpot the root ball, gently tease away the potting mix, and store the bare tubers in crates of vermiculite, just as you would for in-ground tubers.

Just because this season is over, that doesn’t mean you can’t enjoy your dahlias again. A little extra effort now allows you to enjoy these gorgeous blooms year after year. Caring for your dahlias after the first fall frosts doesn’t require special techniques or time-intensive labor. A half hour is all you need to cut back frost-nipped stalks, lever tuber clumps from the earth, and pack them into cozy quarters, or protect them if you leave them where they are. If you do tuck your tubers away this month, you just need to check in on them occasionally over winter Next year, your tubers will be in great shape and fully primed to deliver your most breathtaking blooms yet.

#7903. Want Year-Round Curb Appeal, Even in Winter? Try These 20 Stunning Plants

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Jennifer Noonan, Updated by Teresa Odle

Published Nov 3, 2026 4:30 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Does your home’s landscape look barren and brown after autumn leaves fall, and doesn’t perk back up again until spring? Most homeowners think about how their beds will look when they’re in full bloom, but few imagine how that same bed will look in the dead of winter. Outdoor winter plants that add beautiful contrast to a snowy landscape aren’t just good for your curb appeal—they can also provide critical food sources and nesting sites for wildlife. As you consider updates to the plants and shrubs that surround your home, look to these appealing, year-round options.

Blue Ice bog rosemary’s unique silvery-blue foliage looks good in every season, plus this evergreen ground cover delights with a shock of pink bell-shaped blooms in early spring. Perfect for rock gardens and moist soils, it will attract birds and bring visual interest to the yard all year.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 2 to 6Size: 1 to 2 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Blue Ice Bog Rosemary at The Tree Center for $39.50

This dwarf pine variety turns from green to gold when cold weather arrives. In fact, the colder the climate, the more intense its color becomes. This rabbit- and deer-resistant plant is easy to care for, and an evergreen shrub that will look beautiful all year long. It grows slowly, but immediately adds low-growing color and texture to a winter bed.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 2 to 7Size: nearly 2 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon potted Carstens Wintergold Mugo Pine at Mike’s Plants on Etsy for $75

Many weeping ornamentals lose their leaves in cold weather, but not the weeping Norway spruce. With its unusual shape and showy cones, this evergreen makes a great accent in the garden and provides rich green in all four seasons. It can thrive in many soil types, including rich sandy soils, and has low water needs once established.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 7Size: 4 feet high and 15 feet aroundWhere to buy: Get a 3- to 4-foot high Weeping Norway Spruce at Spring Hill Nurseries for $299

This evergreen succulent creates a lush and attractive carpet that thrives year-round in cool to warm climates. Most boast tiny flowers that attract butterflies in summer, and the foliage of Pink Form and Purple Form can take on reddish to purple hues in colder months. Easy to care for in full sun, this little wonder packs a lot of life in its compact height but excellent spread. After a season or two, it is xeric.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 5 to 9Size: 1 feet high and 1 to 1.5 feet aroundWhere to buy: Get a 4-inch pot of Sedum Hispanicum at Cristina’s Garden on Etsy for $10.99

For evergreen ground cover in warmer climates, try Pot Belly Pittosporum. The tough little shrub flowers in spring and summer, leaving its silvery green foliage with a white underside on the plant through winter.  Best of all, it keeps its rounded shape with little maintenance required. Pot Belly Pittosporum is drought tolerant once established and can grow in partial to full sun.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 8 to 11Size: 4 feet tall and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Pot Belly Pittosporum at Cornell Farm for $28.99

This ground-hugging variety of dianthus is evergreen and cold hardy. Its gray-green foliage erupts in summer with flowers, making it a wonderful filler both in the garden and in pots, so feel free to grow it in a container and overwinter it indoors in colder zones. The flowers are also fragrant, adding a clove-like scent to the garden.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 8Size: about 1 foot high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Frosty Fire Dianthus at Holly Days for $11.99

If you’re looking for a distinctive shade of evergreen color, dwarf globe blue spruce delivers. This slow-growing, densely branched conifer has blue needles that become more brilliant in summer. It makes a wonderful low hedge, or stands out as a small rabbit-resistant shrub.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 4 to 8Size: 2 to 3 feet high and 3 to 4 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Dwarf Globe Blue Spruce tree at Trees.com for $54.95

Pink pussytoe plants provide an evergreen mat of tiny silver-gray leaves. In late spring, the plant spikes deep pink, fuzzy flowers. It’s a slow grower and requires little water once established, so this cold-hardy beauty is a breeze to care for in any season. The native cultivar grows best in full sun.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 8Size: 0.5 feet high and 1 foot wideWhere to buy: Get a bag of 20 Pussytoes seeds at SeedCult on Etsy for $2.99

Snowdrop bulbs are happiest with cold or moderate winters, and are among favorite winter-flowering plants. Place them in full or partial where you can enjoy their delicate white flowers in the fall and throughout the cold months, even during snow. Come spring, they’ll go dormant.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 9Size: 0.5 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a bag of 25 Galanthus Nivalis bulbs at White Flower Farm for $20

Christmas rose, a variety of hellebore, is a pest-resistant evergreen perennial. It also provides valuable nectar for early pollinators, like the rusty patched bumblebee, who are seeking blooms in late winter or early spring. Find it a shady location with space to grow, and soon you’ll enjoy its white winter blooms in the warmer end of their growing range or early spring where colder.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 8Size: 1 foot tall and up to 1.5 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon potted Ivory Prince Christmas Rose at Plant Addicts for $49.99

Winter jasmine is a vining shrub that will treat you with bursts of fragrant yellow flowers between late winter and early spring; the plant’s flowers often are the first to appear as winter wraps up. But even when not in bloom, this plant’s large arching stems will provide plenty of visual interest to the garden. Hardy and easy to grow, winter jasmine is just at home in coastal areas as it is along rock walls.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 6 to 10Size: up to 10 feet tall and 6 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon pot of Winter Jasmine at The Home Depot for $25.58

Known for its medicinal properties, witch hazel is often used in cosmetics and lotions, since it is reported to reduce inflammation and soothe certain skin irritations. It’s also a great choice for a winter garden, thanks to its fragrant yellow-to-red flowers that can bloom even in snowy weather. This adaptable shrub or small tree thrives in full sun to partial shade.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 7Size: 3 to 6 feet tall and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1- to 2-foot high Witch Hazel at TN Nursery for $26.99

Named for its small clusters of white berries that put on a show throughout the winter and give way to little white flowers in the spring, the snowberry plant provides a valuable food source for birds during the cold winter months. This easy-care plant will spread as a dense thicket, so it’s a great choice for borders and living fences.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 9Size: more than 15 feet tall and wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon potted White Snowberry at The Home Depot for $38.04

Featuring dark green glossy leaves, sweet box plants are shade-loving evergreen shrubs that boast small fragrant flowers that bloom in late winter and early spring. Once the fragrant flowers fade, little black fruits will appear in their wake. Preferring partial to full shade, sweet box plants are tough and excellent year-round plants to add interest to the garden.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 6 to 8Size: up to 2 feet high and 4 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Fragrant Dwarf Sweet Box at Planting Partners on Etsy for $28.99

For a vibrant splash of color in warmer zones, plant winter heath in your yard, which will repay you with abundant tiny pink winter flowers that bloom in late winter through early spring. The colorful winter shrub is an even hardier version of E. carnea, and both are commonly used as a ground cover, forming a dense mat. Prune it right after it finishes flowering in the spring to prevent leafless stems and keep it looking great all year.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 6 to 8Size: up to 2 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a quart-size potted Erica Kramer’s Red Winter Heath at The Home Depot for $18.53

This deciduous shrub’s large size creates a show-stopping garden accent. In mid- to late fall, the American cranberry bush will burst with vibrant red berries that last into winter. The berries  are edible but aren’t very tasty when eaten raw. However, they provide important winter food for wildlife. Fragrant while flowers appear in spring and persist through mid summer. The shrub thrives in full or partial sun and prefers alkaline soil.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 2 to 7Size: 8 to 12 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 3-gallon Bailey Compact American Cranberry Bush at Plant Addicts for $73.99

Also known as Perovskia, Russian sage is popular for its tall blue-violet flowers that bloom in the summer through the fall, attracting all sorts of pollinators to the garden. However, this shrub looks great in the winter, too, thanks to long silvery stems that offer structure and intrigue to a winter landscape. Leave the faded flower stems on until new growth appears in spring and plant Russian sage along walkways to maximize enjoyment of its fragrant flowers in summer. Once established, it is a drought-tolerant shrub.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 5 to 9Size: up to 4 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 3-inch potted Lacey Blue Russian Sage at American Meadows for $7.99

Also known as Eastern teaberry, American wintergreen features glossy evergreen leaves and bright red berries that will offer a beautiful contrast to a wintery white landscape. Like many winter outdoor plants, this shrub helps small mammals and birds who love the berries. It is disease-resistant, and crushing its leaves will release a refreshing wintergreen scent. Plant the showy low grower in dappled sunlight to deep shade to keep it happy.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 3 to 7Size: less than 1 foot high and up to 1 foot wideWhere to buy: Get 6 bare root Teaberry Wintergreen plants at New Hampshire Plants on Etsy for $9.99

Yucca glauca is among the most winter-hardy yucca varieties. Its attractive evergreen foliage features long narrow stems in a rosette shape that look great all year long. In the spring, a stem rises from the rosette that features white bell-shaped flowers. These flowers attract butterflies, and the entire easy-care yucca plant provides food and nesting opportunities for small mammals, birds, and reptiles.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 4 to 8Size: 3 to 4 feet high and wideWhere to buy: Get a 5-inch pot of Soapweed Yucca at Etsy for $24.75

This low-growing shrub features glossy dark green leaves that turn bronze in the fall, persisting through the winter. During the winter you’ll also be treated to the shrub’s remaining vivid red berries, which provide a valuable food source for birds. The berries arise from tiny white flowers that form in the spring and summer, which butterflies love. Plant it in full sun to watch it thrive, though the shrub can handle partial shade.

USDA plant hardiness zone: 5 to 8Size: 1 foot high and 4 to 6 feet wideWhere to buy: Get a 1-gallon Bearberry Cotoneaster Coral Beauty at Plants Express for $17.95

The prices listed here are accurate as of publication on November 3, 2026.

#7902. Let’s Be SMART – Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. in Keratea, Greece, is a truly unique organization, currently home to over 100 cats and 13 dogs, living in a cage-free, home-like, villa-style environment. S.M.A.R.T. stands for Successfully Managing Animal Rights Today, and for Julie Kelley, founder and manager of this international animal welfare organization, that means working towards global animal welfare, sharing essential information and facts about animals worldwide, and helping people understand the benefits that come from treating animals with compassion and care.

I had been traveling to Greece since 1998 and would see the issues with stray cats and dogs.  I felt very comfortable in Greece. I had business with Greek nationals in New York, learned a lot of the language, and understood the cultural differences. I felt it was my mission to create Letâs Be S.M.A.R.T. to help people understand the great benefits animals provide to us humans and to educate young people as well. Of course, after a couple of years, it was hard not to take in the first kitty who gave birth, and well, it just grew exponentially from there! Since 2007, we have added many programs and special projects to continue our quest to provide the best we can for our strays.

Letâs be S.M.A.R.T. aims to educate the public about the importance of animals by raising awareness of their rights, well-being, and care. We believe in thinking globally and acting locally by supporting special projects as they arise and, through our programs, bringing communities together to promote responsible animal care.

In Greece, our campaign is primarily centred on reducing the suffering, abuse, and neglect of animals while increasing public awareness of their needs and rights. These include running an innovative and modern foster home, managing a rehoming program for rescued animals, and collaborating with municipalities to implement effective stray animal care initiatives. We also provide practical solutions for supporting strays in urban communitiesâsuch as ensuring access to food and waterâand we actively engage philanthropic individuals who travel to Greece to volunteer, learn about shelter medicine, and receive training in best practices in animal care.

The creation of the sanctuary and setting up the organization in Greece was a huge accomplishment. Let's be S.M.A.R.T. is always evolving with fresh ideas to make life better for the cats and dogs we have in our care.

Our campaign model is unique in Greece. We have created the âSMART Starfish approachâ in which all five arms must function together to create the best outcome.

Each arm of the starfish represents a core pillar of our mission:

Sterilization â controlling population growth at its source

Medical Care & Microchipping â restoring health and identity

Feeding & Shelter â stability, nourishment, and safety

Education & Community â knowledge that shapes future behavior

NGO Collaboration â collective strength through partnership

For years, our programs and ideas have been influencing how animal charities operate and making permanent changes for a better future for animal welfare in Greece.

We created the following programs: Volunteer, SMART Family Video Series, Veterinary Internship, SMART Yards, and Adoption Vacation, all of which are operational every day and are detailed on the Programs page on our website, if you would like to take a closer look. We could not function without the help of our amazing Volunteers.

We successfully found wonderful homes for 73 cats in 2025. I'm not 100% sure, but I would say we are one of the leading cat adopters in Greece!

We receive multiple enquiries from tourists who have found a cat or kitten, and they want to take it home with them to their country. Many times they have cared for them during their stay, provided medicine, bottle-fed babies, etc. This has become increasingly common, with visitors seeing cats all over Greece. Therefore, I decided to offer the Adoption-Vacation as a package. We care for the kitten or cat until it is ready to travel, taking care of the necessary vaccines, passport, microchip, etc. Once the cat is ready to travel, we make travel arrangements with the adopter.

You can see our cats, kittens, and dogs for adoption on our website and have a video chat with us about your requirements and meet a cat if you have already fallen in love (we created a Kitty Picker to help you choose the character of your cat), and then arrange a visit with us when you arrive in Greece. If the home check is secured, we arrange the papers for your new pet to travel home with you. Or we can foster a cat you rescue while you are in Greece and deal with the veterinary needs, papers etc. The cat can travel after you leave with a flight buddy or one of our volunteers.

What better souvenir to have from Greece than a beautiful cat that needed special love and care?

Everything we do is linked. The more sterilizations we achieve, the safer and healthier the animals are in the community; they are interacting better with each other, and people know they are sterilized.

We would like the municipalities and communities all over Greece to enjoy the benefits of the SMART Yards and help take care of the animals. Working together is the future.  We are also collaborating with some officials regarding some policies involving the strays and to help create some standards for housing the strays. Animals and people need to coexist in a humane way. Not every cat needs to be inside a home but can remain cared for and part of our ecosystem.

A rather big goal is to find someone to help us purchase the property we rent, make refurbishments and sustainable features, and add a vet clinic for shared use with other charities and our vet interns. This is a tall order, but we are looking for someone who would like to leave a legacy.

We also want to extend our ability to provide food and shelter after sterilization so that every animal is cared for.

Our animals live in a home-style environment, so every day is the same as if they were living in a family home. Cats are either in bedrooms; we have a retirement room, a special dietary needs room, and a kitten nursery, each with cats that are selected to share a room together, or they are in the main house and free to mingle and hang out on our netted balconies in cute wooden houses and take in the fresh air and nature, since we are in a rural setting, just 15 minutes from Athens International Airport.

Some of the funniest moments are with kittens and playful cats. Plus, bonded pairs â we have a husband-and-wife team called Jasper and Margot who need to be adopted together, and they are very entertaining with their games and spats.

Cats and dogs choose who they like and want to go home with. We find people fall in love with cats that come to them, and a chemistry is formed. Sometimes a visitor leaves, and they cannot stop thinking about the cat they fell in love with and make an application to adopt. We are so happy when this happens. We have repeat adoptions from families and visitors all over the world. We also have Sponsors and Patreon for people to support our work.

Volunteering is open to everyone around the world who would like to come to stay and help us. If you love animals, it's an opportunity to help save lives. It's pure joy to see a cat or dog that was sick transform into good health and finally live in a wonderful family home. That's what the team at Let's be S.M.A.R.T. wants for them all: to be safe, healthy, and happy.

People can also help by following, subscribing, and sharing us on socials. Donations are greatly appreciated, as are supplies, and we created the Amazon Wishlist so gifts can be sent to us directly from Amazon Germany, tax-free.

If youâre visiting Greece and see a lot of stray cats, itâs a good idea to ask around if there is a local organization helping to take care of them. If you see an injured cat, you should immediately try to find a responsible person or contact the local police.

You can also post on local social media groups to try to find help. Most of the cats we take into our foster home settings are from tourists or residents who find our website through a Google search. It is hard to avoid helping, but I would suggest not removing an animal from their setting to a hotel room or Airbnb, and then leaving and putting it back on the street. The cat can get disoriented and perhaps be in danger.

We truly hope to have more controlled community care for our strays in the future.

The Letâs be S.M.A.R.T. organization is a Public Charity registered in the State of New York under the 509 (a) (2) Status and under the Internal Revenue Code (IRC) Section 501 (c) (3); tax ID number is 20-4051556. We are also a registered non-profit organization in Greece.

My professional gardener husband knows better than anyone that roses need a little extra attention before winter arrives...

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

What do roses need in November? As the wife of a professional gardener, I’ve learned that there are just three things these beloved flowers crave from us.

Now, my husband has spent more than 20 years caring for gardens, and he has always had roses (more specifically, hybrid roses) on his unofficial list of plants that he will never let me buy, no matter how much I might beg and plead with him over the matter. That's not to say, though, that he doesn't know how to care for them; he has looked after plenty of these thorny flowers over the past two decades.

So, if you want to keep your own blooming beauties safe during extreme low temperatures and even occasional thaws, look this way...

I love my roses to bits (because yes, I still have a few in my garden – I've just made sure to stick to tougher, more wildlife-friendly roses like Rosa rugosa), but every winter I turn to my husband with wide and pleading eyes whenever the forecast starts muttering about "the big freeze".

Thankfully, his advice is always the same (and always so calmly delivered), and it all hinges on three easy tasks...

My husband's first tip for prepping roses in November is simple enough: look for tall and unruly rose canes. While he never gives his roses a major pruning in November, he does shorten any excessively long growth that could be whipped around by strong winter winds.

"High wind can catch tall growth, violently rocking the plant back and forth in the ground," he explains. "This loosens and tears the root system, often creating a gap at the base where water can pool, freeze, and rot the roots."

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Just remember that this is a protective trim, not an opportunity to reshape the entire bush. Save your main structural pruning for late winter or early spring, when the worst of the cold weather has passed.

"Don't leave that mess sitting around the bottom of your roses. You'll only regret it come spring." This is one adage my husband is particularly strict about, and he always works to remove fallen leaves from around the base of every rose in November – and picks off any diseased foliage still clinging to the stems, too.

The reason? Fungal diseases such as black spot, rust, and powdery mildew can survive on infected plant material, potentially causing problems when warmer, wetter weather returns. "It's much easier to clean it up now than deal with another outbreak next year," he says.

As ever, he's right (although don't tell him I said so). Removing infected foliage and disposing of it appropriately helps reduce the amount of disease-carrying material left around the plants over winter.

"Mulch is your best friend in winter. Never underestimate it."

I know I've heard this a thousand times, but my husband really does swear by it. In colder regions, he recommends making like Martha Stewart when it comes to winterizing roses in November: think mounding mulch around the base of vulnerable roses to protect the crown and graft union from freezing temperatures.

Repeated freezing and thawing can damage exposed roots and even push plants out of the ground. A protective mound, though? Why, that helps insulate these vulnerable areas against temperature fluctuations.

"Just make sure you're protecting the important bit," he tells me. "And don't assume every rose needs the same treatment."

And... well, that's it! "People think roses are difficult," my husband often says, "but most problems start when you don't give them the attention they need."

Honestly, after watching him care for roses year after year? I have to agree. A few simple jobs in November can make all the difference when those first spring shoots appear... even if that just looks like treating yourself to a few new bare root plants and getting them in the ground.

Hey, you deserve a garden full of roses – even if I'm not allowed!

Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

We just sent a welcome email your way with a quick overview of what to expect (including those vital recall alerts).

We often turn to art for pleasure, curiosity, or a feeling we canât quite put into words. A painting catches our attention; a sculpture makes us pause. But art inspiring us to adopt a dog? Now thereâs a plot twist.

The Rescue Collection is an exciting project created through a collaboration between The Sato Project, creative agencies BLKJ Havas Singapore and Havas New York, and Brooklynâs Powerhouse Arts. The program brings adoptable dogs into the art gallery and uses observations of their responses to create individual artistic profiles. The aim is to help potential adopters see the dogs beyond their appearance, breed, or uncertain past.

Itâs an unusual approach to a familiar challenge: helping rescue dogs get noticed in a crowded adoption landscape.

At Powerhouse Arts in Brooklyn, animal welfare scientist Dr. Holly Molinaro observed dogs from The Sato Project as they explored different artworks. The dogs first had time to sniff around and become comfortable in the unfamiliar space. Their responses were then observed, including whether they looked at, sniffed, or moved away from particular pieces, or chose to lie down nearby.

Rudolph, for example, chose to lie down in front of some sculptures but ignored others. These observations helped shape profiles associating the dogs with artistic styles such as Surrealism, Minimalism, Figurative art, and Abstraction.

The concept is playful, but its purpose is practical. A standard adoption photograph may show what a dog looks like; a creative profile offers another reason to stop scrolling and learn more about the animal behind the image.

Someone might come for the art and leave wanting a dog. Turns out, the best thing in the gallery might have four legs and be up for adoption.

The Sato Project rescues dogs in Puerto Rico and helps place them in homes, including in the northeastern United States. Some arrive with limited information about their histories, and assumptions about a dogâs background can influence how potential adopters perceive them.

A dogâs history can help rescue teams understand what support an animal may need and how to approach introductions to a new home. But the past doesnât tell the whole story. A complicated backstory might tell us where a dog has been. It doesnât tell us everything about who they are. Dogs, much like people, are so much more than their basic profile.

Dogs respond to the world as individuals. One may eagerly approach a stranger, while another prefers to observe from a safe distance. Neither reaction alone defines the dogâs personality or tells us what kind of companion they might become with time and appropriate support.

The Rescue Collection offers a different starting point. Instead of focusing on what is known about a dogâs past, it invites people to become curious about the dog in front of them. That first spark of interest can matter, especially for dogs who might otherwise be overlooked.

Dogs explore their surroundings through several senses, and their behavior around unfamiliar objects can offer clues about what attracts their attention. But interpreting those responses requires care.

Dogs also see color differently from humans. People typically have three types of color-sensitive cone cells in their retinas, while dogs have two, a form of vision known as dichromacy. Dogs distinguish blues and yellows relatively well but have more difficulty differentiating reds and greens. Their visual experience of the world is therefore different from ours.

That doesnât mean dogs see the world in black and white. Color is only one possible influence on how they respond to an object. Shape, contrast, texture, scent, movement, and the surrounding environment may also play a part.

Nor does spending longer near a sculpture necessarily mean a dog prefers its artistic style. The dog may be interested in its shape or position, or simply feel comfortable resting there.

A single gallery visit cannot establish an animalâs overall personality or predict how they will behave around children, other dogs, or visitors at home. Behavior is best understood across time and situations.

A sculpture might have us admiring its color and form. The dog? They might be more interested in giving it a sniff. Different critics, different criteria.

Although the profiles are not scientific personality assessments or guarantees of compatibility, they do invite us to learn more about each dog. Conversations with the rescue team and time spent meeting the dog remain essential to finding a suitable match.

Rescue work involves far more than finding adopters. Veterinary care, foster placements, transportation, behavioral support, and follow-up all require time and resources. Helping the public connect with the dogs is only one part of that work, but an important one.

The Sato Projectâs adoption and foster manager, Alessandra Migliore, said the organization was excited to explore new ways of showcasing its dogsâ personalities. The campaign is part of the organizationâs broader work to help dogs rescued in Puerto Rico find homes in the northeastern United States.

A creative campaign cannot guarantee adoption, and an appealing profile is only the beginning. But an unexpected introduction may reach someone who wasnât actively looking for a dog, or encourage a prospective adopter to look beyond their first impressions.

The Rescue Collection hopes to help more rescue dogs connect with potential adopters. Its message says it best: âSee the masterpiece inside every dog.â

Art might catch someoneâs eye, but getting to know the dog is what matters. And if a sculpture-loving visitor leaves the gallery thinking about adoption, thatâs a pretty good review.

Explore The Rescue Collection, use its rescue-finding tool to search by city or postcode, or meet dogs waiting for homes through The Sato Project.

There are a number of reasons cats tend to be picky when it comes to mealtime. Depending on your feline, you may be dealing with one or all of these difficult instincts and sensitivities.

To start, cats have a very sensitive sense of smell. Even quality food can be turned down if the aroma is too unfamiliar. Cats are also very finicky about textures. They tend to develop very specific preferences about how foods should feel in their mouth. This makes it both hard to introduce new foods and to keep your cat from getting bored with the very specific foods they like.

Many cats exhibit neophobiaâa fear of new things. This doesnât just apply to new people, places, and toys, either. Cats evolved to be naturally wary of new food items and prey. This is likely because their ancestors lived in the desert where many little creatures are deadlier than their size might indicate. While modern cat food isnât likely to be venomous, your cat's instincts still tell them to beware anything they havenât eaten before.

Itâs the combination of a desire for the familiar and a tendency to get bored of the too familiar that makes picky cats so hard to feed. They want enough options that fall within a very specific range of flavors, textures, and aromas to keep them both interested and comfortable.

This can make adding moisture to their diets challenging, too, especially for cats who prefer dry food over wet. Luckily, simple additions like savory bone broth can help cat parents incorporate more moisture without introducing an entirely unfamiliar meal.

Air filters for furnace and home AC are designed to trap dust, dirt, bacteria, and other small particles. Depending on the MERV rating of the house air filter (which measures how well a filter removes particles), it may even be able to trap viruses and other microscopic debris. By removing contaminants from the air, the furnace filtration system improves indoor air quality and protects the internal components of the furnace and AC from the pollutants the return duct takes in.

Furnace and air conditioner filter replacement is essential for the ongoing health of the HVAC system. Our top choice is the Simply Filters 14x25x1 MERV 11 Air Filter, which is designed to trap dust, mold, pet dander, pollen, and even auto exhaust. Additionally, this replaceable air filter has a pleated and electrostatic construction for trapping contaminants, and it works with most furnace and AC brands. Use this guide to learn more about air filter replacement and discover our selection of the best air filters for furnace and home AC.

Bottom line: Choosing the right air filter enhances indoor air quality and HVAC efficiency. Consider MERV ratings, filter types, and proper sizing for optimal results.

Each air filter has a pleated and electrostatic design that attracts and traps dust and debris as small as 1 micron. The high pleat count improves capture coverage while optimizing airflow and air filtration efficiency for up to 3 months before the filter needs to be replaced. Furnace and air conditioner filters are integral to the ongoing operation of the HVAC system, so it’s important to find out what you might not know about HVAC air filters. Learning more about air filters for furnace filtration can help you determine what to look for when choosing a furnace filter’s replacement, including the type of air filter and MERV rating, as well as furnace and air conditioner filter sizes.

Before picking up the first air filter you find, it’s a good idea to determine which type of air filter is best for the home and existing HVAC system. Even the best HVAC brands typically offer a variety of air filter options to choose from, so it’s recommended to learn more about home air conditioner filters, including washable, disposable, fiberglass, pleated, electrostatic, and polyester air filters.

Even the best energy-efficient air conditioners will suffer if they are not equipped with an appropriate air filter. Deciding on the right air filter can be difficult, though, without understanding the terms used to measure the filtration quality and efficiency. MERV stands for minimum efficiency reporting value, which is a number assigned to a product based on its density and filtration capabilities.

Andrew Hulsebos, service director for Reiner Group, a heating and air conditioning company in northern New Jersey, says that the MERV rating system ranges from 1 to 20, and that higher numbers indicate a higher level of filtration. “For residential use, air filters are typically rated between MERV 5 to 13.” Higher-efficiency filters are mainly used in commercial settings or health facilities that are equipped with powerful HVAC systems that are capable of drawing the air through the dense filters.

Furnace and AC air filters are available in a wide range of sizes and thicknesses, so it’s necessary to check the HVAC system operating manual to determine the right size for your system. Generally, if the filter needs to be bent, jammed, or otherwise forced into position, it’s too big. Similarly, the air filter may be too small if it doesn’t come within an inch of all four corners of the air handler slot or frame.

The easiest way to determine the right size air filter for the home is to check the existing air filter. The measurements are usually listed on the frame of the filter, making it easy to find the size. Alternatively, you can measure the existing air filter with a tape measure, or even measure the air intake slot to find out the appropriate size air filter for the HVAC system.

Homeowners will want to stay on top of a range of maintenance tasks to keep the home functional and comfortable, but knowing exactly what needs to be done isn’t always obvious. Before purchasing replacement air filters for furnaces and home AC, it’s worth checking out the answers below to some of the most frequently asked questions about HVAC air filters.

Yes, furnaces and AC units generally use the same air filter. “They share the same air handler, where the filter is located, which means you don’t need to worry about buying separate filters for each system,” says Hulsebos.

Yes. The most common HVAC configuration for residential properties typically involves the furnace and air conditioner sharing the same air filter, so to properly maintain the air conditioner, the furnace filter will need to be replaced or washed when necessary. How often to replace an air filter depends on the number of people and pets, and the frequency with which the home is used. On average, though, you should replace the filter about every 3 months.

The number of air filters in a house tends to depend on the size of the home, including the square footage, number of floors, and the number of HVAC units. Generally, a single air filter is enough for most residential properties, though larger homes may have more than one HVAC unit, each requiring at least one air filter.

HEPA air filters are often considered high-quality products with excellent filtration capabilities. However, Hulsebos notes that “part of the reason that HEPA filters are so rarely used in HVAC systems is that they are extremely restrictive in terms of airflow.” HEPA filters can also be expensive, difficult to clean, and typically need to be replaced every 6 to 12 months.

Residential HVAC systems usually require a filter with a MERV rating between 5 and 13. Air filters with higher MERV ratings may be able to filter smaller particles, but they may put unnecessary stress on the HVAC system as the blower attempts to force the air through the dense filter. So while a higher MERV rating can be better, the air filter needs to be paired with a suitable HVAC system for optimal performance.

Generally, the maximum MERV rating for a residential furnace is 13, though commercial or health care facilities may have more powerful HVAC systems that can operate normally while using air filters up to MERV 20.

The most commonly used air filter in an HVAC system is a pleated air filter. This is because it has high filtration capabilities and a relatively low price. These air filters can generally be purchased online or from a local home improvement store, though some grocery stores may also carry pleated air filters.

#7897. 7 Foolproof Plants Anyone Can Propagate From Cuttings in November – Grow More of Your Favorite Shrubs for Free

There is no easier way to make new plants for free than by taking hardwood cuttings from deciduous shrubs in late fall. Try it yourself and see!

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

November doesn't have to mean the end of the gardening season, as late fall is the perfect time to multiply your backyard shrubs for free. Taking hardwood cuttings sounds complicated but it’s as simple as poking sticks into pots of soil and waiting for them to grow. Yes, really! November is the very best time for this propagation method as stems of deciduous shrubs are full of stored energy ready to go into winter so you'll get great results, even if you're a beginner gardener or it's your first time trying.

Many of our favorite garden shrubs can be multiplied by taking cuttings in late fall, from roses to butterfly bush, dogwood to mock orange, so add this enjoyable task to your fall gardening checklist. Whether you’ve got a new garden to fill on a budget or you’re planting up a fresh area, or you want to propagate some plants to sell at a yard sale next year, you'll get free shrubs without spending a dime at the garden center. Or perhaps you’ve been eyeing up a pretty shrub in a friend’s garden and want it growing in your yard, too!

Clone these deciduous shrubs now and they’ll root over winter, ready to be planted in spring. Ready to have a go? Here’s exactly how to take hardwood cuttings, step by step.

Timing is everything when you propagate plants, and late fall is peak time for growing free shrubs from hardwood cuttings. In November, deciduous shrubs will be about to enter dormancy so they’ll have stored up plenty of energy in their stems and the bare outer bark is tough and weather-resistant. To catch the optimum moment, wait until your shrub has just dropped its leaves or, in a mild autumn, lost a good three quarters of its foliage.

Look for stems that grew this year, as these are going to be far keener to throw out fresh roots than older growth. Choose stems from the outer, sunniest side of the shrub, too, as these will have stored more energy. Stems that are about the width of a standard pencil are ideal, and remember these are hardwood cuttings: you need stems that are mature enough to snap rather than softly bend if you tried to fold them in half.

You’re going to need straight-ish stem sections, and cut plenty as not even expert gardeners get a 100% success rate from hardwood cuttings.

Make the base cut just below a bud or leaf node, straight across the stem. Make this cut close to the node – ⅛ inch below is perfect – as there's a high concentration of rooting cells and hormones in the stem here. Make the top cut about ¼ inch above a bud or leaf node, at a 45° angle. This little bit of extra room allows the stem to heal over without damaging the node. Ideally, you want 2-3 nodes in between the top and bottom nodes (so 5 in total). For most shrubs, that means your stem sections will be 6-12 inches long.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

While the top cut is angled to encourage rain to run off rather than pool on the step tip, the base cut is horizontal simply so it’s easy to tell which end of your cutting is which. Use your pruners to trim off any remaining foliage (don’t tear leaves off as this can damage the stem).

Rooting your cuttings in deep containers rather than the ground makes it easy to provide the sharp drainage and shelter needed for stems to root rather than rot. You can either use one pot per cutting or put multiple cuttings into a bigger container.

Use an all-purpose potting soil without any added fertilizer or synthetic moisture retainers such as Organic Mechanics Premium Blend Potting Soil, available from Amazon, and mix in a similar volume of horticultural grit, sand or perlite such as this from Walmart to open up that soil some more.

Water the mix and leave the pots to sit for 15 minutes to drain.

Use a stick or pencil to poke holes into the potting mix, making them deep enough to swallow two-thirds of the stem length. If you're using a larger container to hold multiple cuttings, space the holes about 2 inches apart. Then pop the stems, base cut downwards, into the holes and use your fingers to gently close the soil around them. There’s no need to water.

Some shrubs have a high-enough concentration of natural auxins – the hormones that foster rooting – that they'll root just fine, all by themselves. Twig dogwood, forsythia, butterfly bush and spirea all fall into this category. Some shrubs need a little help, however. Roses are still reliable rooters, but encouraging them with a rooting powder that stimulates their natural hormones brings a higher success rate. Simply dip the base of the stem into a rooting hormone like Garden Safe Take Root, available from Amazon, and tap off any excess before popping it into the hole.

A few, like mock orange and viburnum, need an even bigger nudge, and that’s easy to deliver by slicing off a narrow inch-long strip of bark at the stem's base before dipping it into the rooting powder, and popping it into the hole. This ‘scoring’ cuts through the tough outer bark to expose the green cambium layer beneath, which is where the cells that will become roots are concentrated. Scoring also triggers auxins to be sent straight to the damaged area.

Stand your pots of cuttings in a sheltered spot where they’re shielded from the worst of the winter rain and cold. Position them up against a south-facing wall of your house and they’ll be protected from cold northerly winds and benefit from the heat escaping your home. An unheated greenhouse, conservatory or sunroom is another good option, as is a bright porch. You could also cover your cuttings with lightweight horticultural fleece such as this AgFabric Plant Blanket from The Home Depot to keep them cozy, pushing canes around the pot so the fabric doesn’t sit directly on the stems.

The stems will use very little water so only irrigate occasionally when the top inch or two of the soil is dry, which will only be once a month or so. By spring, you’ll see fresh green leaves on the cuttings that have rooted. If you're growing multiple cuttings in one big pot, move them into their own container at this point.

Shrub dogwoods or twig dogwoods are super-easy to propagate from hardwood cuttings in late fall, and grow fast for quick results. Why not raise enough to create a wildlife-friendly hedge with a flurry of fragrant spring-summer flowers followed by fall berries? Or create a vibrant display of winter stems for you to enjoy? Cornus has a high concentration of natural rooting compounds so you’ll enjoy a near 100% success rate from hardwood cuttings.

This bulletproof shrub is one of the earliest to bloom in spring, bursting into a cheery show of bright yellow flowers in March. Once mature, Forsythia is drought-tolerant, cold-hardy and incredibly low maintenance, and even copes with urban pollution, making it a welcome gift for beginner gardeners or new home owners. Forsythia's easy-going nature also makes this one of the easiest shrubs to propagate from hardwood cuttings.

Buddleia earned its common name for good reason, putting on a bountiful summer buffet for pollinators from July to October. Butterfly bush is an enthusiastic, fast grower so it’s a useful shrub to quickly make a new garden look more mature, or fill an empty yard corner. Do check that the Buddleia you’re taking cuttings from is a newer, non-invasive butterfly bush variety first though. There is no easier shrub to take hardwood cuttings from as this is a plant that’s naturally programmed to grow, grow, grow!

Spirea is a low-maintenance must-have, bringing fabulous flowers and fall foliage colors in a size to suit every garden. This deciduous shrub responds really well to clipping so you can use it to create a stylish low hedge for free by taking November cuttings. Spirea is a foolproof shrub to start with if you're propagating this way for the first time.

You can never have too many roses in a garden and these shrubs are expensive to buy, so propagating from cuttings will fill your yard with scented flowers for free. The ‘backyard rule’ means you can propagate even named, patented Rosa for your own use, but restrictions apply if you’re planning on selling the resulting plants. While your new rose plant will probably try to flower in its first summer, pinch off any flower buds to focus its energy on growing roots and stems.

Philadelphus brings an aromatic blend of jasmine and citrus to your garden from May to June, so adding a few more mock orange shrubs to your yard will boost its perfume as well as flower power. Mock orange shrubs have tough bark so carefully scrape an inch-long strip off both sides of the stem base and dip into rooting powder to stimulate root growth, and don't worry if cuttings take their time to show spring growth.

The viburnum family includes so many garden-worthy deciduous shrubs such as snowball bush (Viburnum opulus) and the Arrowwood viburnum (Viburnum dentatum) that are straightforward to propagate from hardwood cuttings. Viburnum go into deep winter dormancy however, so also need a boost to root. Score by removing an inch-long strip of bark from the base (one side is plenty) and dip into rooting powder to trigger the stem into action.

Clean cuts made with sharp pruner blades significantly increase your chances of success as crushing stems with blunt pruners damages the plant tissue and creates jagged surfaces where fungal spores can settle.

Wipe isopropyl alcohol over pruner blades to disinfect before cutting stems or scoring, to make sure you’re not transferring any fungal spores or bacteria that might cause rotting rather than rooting.

Winter stems can look identical so be sure to label those sticks clearly so you know what your plants are in spring. These hook-ring tags are useful if you’re rooting cuttings of different varieties in one big pot.

You see, you really are growing free plants by sticking stems into soil, so add this to your list of November gardening jobs. You can put a heap of cuttings into the same pot to propagate plenty of plants without spending a fortune on compost, too. Looking after hardwood cuttings takes minimal time over winter, and it’s so satisfying to spot bare stems bursting into leaf in spring. And just wait till you discover how much more you love a favorite plant when you’ve propagated it yourself!

If you want to propagate plants that are growing outside of your garden, do be aware of the legalities of taking plant cuttings from public spaces and get permission from the landowner.

#7895. Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box Review 2026: Our Expert’s Opinion

We give the Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box a rating of 4.8 out of 5 stars.

Automatic litter boxes are not just a serious time saver for cat owners; theyâre also hugely beneficial for cats, particularly those that refuse to use anything but a fresh bed of cat litter. Yet, some cat parents are hesitant about the idea of bringing home a self-cleaning litter box.

For cats accustomed to an airy, open litter tray, a compact, closed-in automatic litter box might seem like too much of a change. But itâs not always just the cat that has to be convinced. For those accustomed to the simplicity of a basic litter tray, the idea of one with a power cord and moving parts may feel a bit overwhelming.

Whether your hesitation for buying an automatic litter box comes from your fears or your catâs, the Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box has you covered. This unique self-cleaning litter box is designed with an open-air feel to accommodate both large and claustrophobic kitties, and its âsafe by structureâ will give nervous owners total peace of mind.

I had a chance to test the new M9 with my big kitty, Makoa. Keep reading to find out if the clever design of this litter box really makes a difference in my full Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box review below.

In my experience, there are two big reasons cat parents hesitate to make the switch from a traditional litter pan to a fancy self-cleaning litter box.

The first reason is all about the cat. Many owners fear that their cat wonât be able to adjust to the design of an automatic litter box. While traditional tray boxes are wide open on top and allow plenty of room for big cats to turn around, dig, and stand tall as they do their business, most automatic boxes are more compact.

These boxes typically have hoods or are fully enclosed. Many also have smaller litter areas, which can be difficult for larger cats to navigate.

The second issue that keeps many parents scooping manually rather than investing in a box that can do it for them is about safety.

Automatic litter boxes have a lot of moving parts. Many turn completely upside down while cleaning, so itâs natural to be worried that your cat could be frightened, pinched, or trapped by the mechanism. Of course, these boxes have

sensors and safety controls to minimize the risks of an accident, but no technology is foolproof.

With their new automatic litter box, Neakasa listened to the most common concerns of hesitant cat parents and used them to inspire their design.

For the big or claustrophobic kitty, the M9 offers a wide-open, spacious design. The bowl-shaped hood isnât as open as a traditional pan without a roof, but the tilted angle and wide mouth make it much easier for large cats to navigate. And plenty of headspace means even big kitties like Maine Coons and Ragdolls can stand up tall while they do their business.

For the claustrophobic kitty, the M9 has another trick up its sleeve: the hood and âcabinâ of the litter box are translucent. This means plenty of light gets inside, and your cat has the ability to see all around them while they assume that oh-so vulnerable position.

The Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box also has plenty of reassuring features for even the most nervous owner.

This box has many of the same safety sensors that most other automatic boxes do. These work to prevent cleaning while the cat is present and stop cleaning if your cat leaps inside mid-cycle. But what makes the M9 different is that it is structurally designed to be safe even if those sensors fail.

Thanks to the spherical design and âtilt-safeâ rotation, even if the box were to somehow enter cleaning mode while your cat was inside, they would just get a bit of a ride (like a kitty in a hamster ball). Because the M9 cabin is free of pinch points and the opening does not close or shrink during cleaning, it would be virtually impossible for a cat to be harmed.

This is exactly the kind of fail-safe design nervous cat parents need.

Founded in 2017 as Neabot, Neakasa is a smart home and pet-care technology brand headquartered in Shenzhen, China, with offices in Los Angeles and Tokyo.

Its products aim to simplify everyday cleaning and pet care. Beyond automatic litter boxes, Neakasa offers pet grooming kits with vacuum technology, smart pet water fountains, and even air-purifying litter box steps.

As you can guess, the Neakasa M9 Automatic Litter Box is a great option for larger kitties and those who arenât likely to enjoy the cramped quarters of traditional automatic litter boxes. Itâs also great for safety-conscious owners.

Crystal litter, tofu litter, and mixed litter are not recommended, as they may interfere with the automatic cleaning process.

The Neakasa M9 comes with everything needed to get started, including the litter box, a PureTower odor-control filter, a roll of 16 waste-drawer liners, five litter-emptying bags, and a power cord and adapter. It also includes a protective kitten guard, a quick-start guide, and a user manual.

My 12-pound Domestic Shorthair, Makoa, and I have tested a lot of automatic litter boxes in our time, and I can say with all honesty that the M9 from Neakasa is a true standout.

The litter box arrived in a rather large box with a somewhat overwhelming number of parts. But I promise you that it looks much harder than it is to put this together. Following the quick installation guide, I had it up and ready to go in less than ten minutes.

I set the M9 up in the laundry room next to his current automatic cat box, which is a more typical robot cat box with an enclosed cabin and full roof design.
