Kate Hudson’s silver, bronze, and gold bow tree is a nostalgic Christmas look. Experts share how to get it right without it feeling dated.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's official; Kate Hudson’s Christmas tree from last year is still inspiring holiday decorations in 2026.

It's hardly a surprise. After all, the actress (best known for her starring turns in Bride Wars and How to Lose a Guy in 10 Days) kept her Christmas tree simple, classy, and very less is more: think silver, bronze and gold bows, a few ornaments and not much else.

Now, a bow is almost as Christmassy as it gets, whether it’s tied on a tree, a wreath or a present. A nostalgic tree does have one risk, though: if you do it without thinking it through, it can go from warm and charming to dated really quickly. Some experts gave me tips on how you can avoid this, and get Kate Hudson’s Christmas tree look.

For those who have yet to see Kate Hudson's Christmas tree in all its glory, flick your eyes downwards...

A post shared by Kate Hudson (@katehudson)

It feels like a rebellion against the minimalist matchy-matchy (and beige) trend that has been going on for so many years, doesn't it? “People are tired of the same old, store-bought, themed trees,” says Irena Cara, interior designer and co-founder of Nova Wrap.

Reilly Renwick, designer and creative lead of State of the Wall, points to Millennial parents whose kids are now the age they were in the 1990s. Many of them, he says, want to revive “the warm, festive and childlike vibe of a 90s Christmas, as opposed to what people are now calling the ‘sad beige’ of contemporary tree styling.”

So, how best to recreate it? Other than buying some of this beautiful metallic gold ribbon from Amazon. We have a few ideas...

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Hey, we might not have Goldie Hawn as a mum, but when it comes to Christmas nostalgia, a lot of millennials remember our parents' houses being packed with all kinds of stuff, and so much color that it felt cluttered. So, the biggest worry with going with a nostalgic look is the tree looking tacky.

For Renwick, “the biggest challenge for anyone trying to create a nostalgic tree is how to evade the ‘tacky’ accusations.” His answer is to look at what Kate Hudson did with hers. “The whole point of this ‘comeback’ thing is to evoke the festive vibe of the 90s, not to recreate it in painstaking detail,” he says.

Shop Nostalgic Christmas Tree Essentials:

Want the Kate Hudson look? “My advice is to use the metallic bows with restraint, in such a way that they stand out but still leave space for the other decorations and the tree itself to still be visible,” says Renwick.

Cara has practical tips for gold, silver, and bronze. “Use brushed or matte ribbon to take the ‘shiny’ edge off, especially if the metals are varying warm tones. Also, make sure the bows are of varying sizes, to keep things interesting.”

For quantity, she says: “On a tree between 6 and 7 feet, use between 20 and 30 bows.” Lighting matters too: “Warm white lights make metallics look even better.”

A Christmas tree runs the risk of feeling tacky, true, but it can also feel too generic, like it should be in a department store in the 90s. Nadi Melam, founder of Florals Memories, has a way to avoid this.

“You can’t purchase nostalgia, but you can tie it!” she says. Her suggestion is to reuse ribbon that already means something. “Use ribbons that have a story, such as paper that a bouquet you received came wrapped in. On the loose end of the ribbon, write down the date you received it, and now your tree is a timeline.”

Melam preserves flowers for a living, so she also suggests pairing a ribbon with a flower from your own garden. She says you can build the look slowly: “You can add one more ribbon to your tree each year.”

If you already have tons of ornaments that have been passed down by family or maybe something your kids have made, bows can tie them into a whole scheme.

Cara says to put the old pieces where people look first: “Place heirloom and vintage pieces at eye level in the center where people look first.” Then, let the ribbon link everything together. “Match the ribbon to details on the older ornaments, such as a gold edge or a red glass.”

A big advantage of a bow tree like Kate Hudson's is that it’s very cheap to update, as ribbon is super easy to swap out for different colors and patterns. “Swap out the ribbon and keep the ornaments to change decorations year to year for a small cost,” says Cara.

Melam says to store ribbon carefully between seasons: “Moisture and light will cause your ribbon to fade, so store it flat in a cool, dark, dry place.”

Kate Hudson’s tree works because it feels warm and traditional without trying to look like a time capsule. Keep your color palette tight and give your ribbon some history to recreate the same nostalgia.

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

There’s always something new and exciting on the horizon in the world of gardening. Around this time every year, various organizations release their favorite gardening and landscaping trends for the coming year. From the color of the year to new plants and outdoor décor, the list below represents our favorite 2027 gardening trends for you to consider as you plan or update your outdoor space in the coming months.

Garden Media Group has identified ancient blue as the garden color of the year for 2027. As the first manufactured color in history, blue was created by the Egyptians 5,000 years ago to imitate precious lapis lazuli. While blue is consistently the favorite color around the world, it is the rarest color in the garden, showing up in fewer than 10 percent of flowers. “This makes growing it in the garden feel like victory,” says Katie Dubow, president of Garden Media Group.

Here are some planting and décor tips to seamlessly incorporate this calming color into your garden:

Gardeners prefer more from their edible plants than just fruits and vegetables to harvest, according to Monrovia’s 2027 Garden Design Trends Study. “We’re seeing shoppers be more discerning in their edible choices,” says Katie Tamony, chief marketing officer and trend spotter at Monrovia. “They’re looking for plants that add a design element or feel more exotic than the common choices their neighbors grow. People are also interested in edible plants that look good all season long.”

Adding an edible garden ranks among the highest-interest projects in Monrovia’s survey, with more than 45 percent of respondents saying they are looking for more unique selections. Enhance your edible garden with specialty herbs; berries with year-round interest; and conversation-starting selections like pomegranate, figs, kiwi, and olives.

After years of beige minimalism and tidy rows of shrubs, the “Let’s Go Rococo” theme is all about exuberance over restraint, says Dubow. Emerging in early 18th century France, rococo design was a deliberate rebellion by artists and craftsmen against the stiff grandeur of Baroque and societal wealth inequality. Think flowers, shells, gilded flourishes, ruffles, jewel-tone palettes, and asymmetry. “It’s ornamental, romantic, a little over the top, and joyful,” notes Dubow.

Here are some ways to infuse rococo style into your garden:

Garden Media Group’s OutdooRx trend positions the garden as medicine, says Dubow. “In the United Kingdom, doctors now “socially prescribe” gardening programs to patients, and research continues to show that gardening lowers stress hormones like cortisol while boosting mood-lifting dopamine and serotonin,” she explains. Approaches like the Sunday Garden Trend can provide relaxation.

Fortunately, you don’t need a prescription to benefit. You can create a therapeutic garden in your own backyard with these helpful tips:

This long-handle digging tool allows gardeners to work the soil more comfortably (and for longer periods of time) from a standing position.

National Garden Bureau also tracks garden trends, especially when it comes to which specific plants are the most popular in a given year. “Coming up in 2027, we see an enormous interest in hellebores, and that is our Year of the Crop for Perennials,” says Diane Blazek, executive director for All-America Selections at National Garden Bureau.

Often called the Christmas rose or Lenten rose, the hellebore is a hardy perennial that does well in full shade and brings beauty to winter and early spring gardens when most other flowers have faded. It produces elegant 2- to 3-inch blossoms in a cup shape that resemble roses. Hellebore flowers grow in a variety of colors, so you have plenty of options. It grows in USDA Hardiness Zones 5 to 8, and does best in cottage gardens, winter gardens, or woodland gardens. Take note that this plant is toxic and should be handled with caution.

As another season of the popular show The Gilded Age is released this month, romance and beauty are alive and well in gardens, too. This look maximizes the popularity of European-inspired garden design with an elevated, modern twist, shining a spotlight on classic plants like roses, peonies, hydrangeas, and boxwood. In addition to these timeless plants, this trend showcases artful hedges, chartreuse foliage, and collector statement plants.

“This trend appeals to established gardeners,” says Tamony. “Homeowners who have invested in their interior design are taking that high-end look to the garden.” Their interest in rare, collector plants is increasing, and Monrovia’s research shows their willingness to pay for premium plants and exquisite blooms is up between 5 and 9 percent since 2025.

Another style that is expected to be popular is the Palm Springs outdoor space. This works well for gardeners looking to create an attractive desert oasis through containers as well as the landscape. “The Palm Springs Style trend is all about creating a calming, wellness-focused outdoor space that feels more upscale,” says Tamony. With this aesthetic, gardeners can transform their landscape by choosing structured succulents and lush, tropical colors found with species from Agave, Bougainvillea, Mandevilla, and tropical hibiscus.

#7829. Some of My Favorite Evergreen Shrubs Just Went on Sale at Home Depot – and They'll Keep Your Garden Looking Good Year-Round

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Beautiful plants and ideas to brighten your garden.

Expert tips for growing fruit, vegetables and herbs at home.

Sign up to get fresh gardening ideas, inspiration and expert advice delivered straight to your inbox.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

All-year backyard structure on a budget? Yes please! Evergreen shrubs are the landscape-design must every garden is missing, and these can all be planted now.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As leaves drop in fall, I always wish I’d planted more evergreen shrubs in my garden to give structure and color all through the winter. From tall arborvitae cones to slender columns of holly and perfect no-prune spheres, evergreens give a garden a shapely skeleton on which to hang seasonal blooms. While I’m lucky enough to have mature yew hedges and an old conifer I’m planning to cloud-prune, I want to add evergreen accents to borders and alongside a path to punctuate my garden design. Globes of green leaves in patio planters are high on my wish list too.

What's stopped me? One of the basic principles of garden design is to always repeat-plant evergreens in odd numbers – and bying multiple plants gets expensive, fast. But Home Depot must have been listening in to my garden-design dreams because it’s not even Thanksgiving yet and a heap of my favorite evergreen shrubs just had their prices slashed in an early Black Friday plant sale. And frankly, the prices were pretty decent even before they went on sale.

Let’s skip straight to the good bit, shall we?

While most boxwood shrubs grow incredibly slowly, sprinter boxwood lives up to its name, meaning you can buy a smaller, cheaper plant. And don’t worry that Buxus microphylla will grow too big because it maxes out at 2-4 feet high and wide: large enough to have an impact in your yard without taking over. Sprinter boxwood keeps its glossy green foliage year-round and has excellent resistance to diseases and pests, including boxwood blight. Suitable for zones 4-9, this handsome shrub is easily shaped to create structural evergreen mounds in a border, a low square hedge or appealing spheres in planters.

Thuja occidentalis ‘Anna van Vloten’ is a dwarf evergreen that naturally grows in a compact sphere without ever needing to be clipped. With wonderfully textural fan-like foliage, it keeps a bright golden-green tone year-round and grows well in zones 3-8. Anna’s Magic Ball arborvitae only grows to 10-15 inches high and wide and looks delightful dotted through a border. If you’re looking for compact shrubs to boost your curb appeal or want to add some stylish year-round planters to your patio, here’s the easy solution.

Here’s another dwarf cultivar of Thuja occidentalis that naturally grows in a compact ball shape without requiring any pruning. Danica America arborvitae is a little bigger at 2 feet high and wide and a brighter green, but what really sets it apart is its fan-like foliage that grows in vertical layers. The evergreen foliage is denser than Anna’s Magic Ball, too. Use it to create a smart geometric accent alongside a path or add stylish structure to a border without taking up too much space. It's one of the best evergreens for containers, too, and suitable for zones 3-7.

For instant style in zones 6-9, few evergreen shrubs have the striking aplomb of sky pencil holly. It’s a cultivar of the lovely Japanese holly and while it grows 6-10 feet tall, it stays a slender 1-2 feet wide with unusual vertical branches. The leaves are small, glossy and dark green – more like a boxwood than a holly – so the growth is dense, accentuating the shape. So, while sky pencil holly doesn’t boast red berries (though it does grow small black berries in fall), its silhouette provides more than enough drama. Happy in a large planter or in well-drained ground, sky pencil holly looks fabulous either side of a doorway or gate, or planted in a loose line, and is one of the best shrubs for a front yard.

So far, so green. And while it’s wonderful to have shrubs that bring texture and a year-round skeleton of leaves, some evergreen shrubs also deliver a generous splash of color. And Encore azalea is one of the very best flowering plants to add to your garden in fall. While many azaleas are deciduous, and older varieties only flower for a few short weeks in spring, the Encore series not only keeps its leaves through winter but repeat-blooms all through spring, summer and autumn. It maintains a tidy, rounded shape so requires very little pruning, and there are all sorts of flower colors to choose from. Suitable for zones 6-10, Autumn Royalty has bright magenta blooms and you’ll also find Autumn Lily with white flowers, Autumn Carnation with pink flowers, and Autumn Embers with red-orange flowers in Home Depot’s sale.

Euonymus fortunei ‘Roemertwo’ is one of those easy wins that every garden needs, requiring little looking after but working hard four seasons of the year. Don't be put off by the fact it's a wintercreeper as this cultivar is a compact mounding shrub. Its evergreen foliage doesn’t lose its variegation and revert to green like many shrubs, and thank goodness because the lime-green leaves have lovely gold margins that positively glow on a dark winter day. Adding to the color, Gold Splash wintercreeper boasts yellow fruit that open to reveal orange seeds in fall. Highly resistant to disease, this neat, ultra-tough shrub reaches 18-24 inches high and wide in zones 5-8.

Okay, so Viburnum nudum ‘Brandywine’ isn’t evergreen but it does look good all through winter on account of the multi-colored berries that cling to the branches months after leaves have fallen. Brandywine viburnum is one of the best berry-bearing shrubs to feel birds through winter as its berries only sweeten once the worst winter weather sets in, providing a valuable late-season pantry for our feathered friends. Those berries provide quite a show, too, starting green then shifting through pink and blue to a glossy dark purple. Hardy in zones 5-9, this low-maintenance shrub reaches 5-6 feet high.

Whether it’s for security or style, investing in solar gutter lights is an affordable way to upgrade any home. Though they aren’t quite as easy to install as solar lanterns, most solar gutter lights are generally easy to put up, typically attaching via clips to a home’s gutters. They can be installed as temporary or permanent fixtures that convert the day’s sun into attractive lighting on the exterior of a home. Many lights also include additional mounting hardware so they can be used above doorways, along fence posts, and as deck lights, making them both solar security lights and architectural features on a home’s exterior.

We recently hands-on tested five sets of solar gutter lights against 2 weeks of wind, rain, and plenty of sunshine to see how they held up. While the price of solar gutter lights can be a factor, appearance and durability take center stage. And because these lights are frequently installed at high points on a home, low maintenance is key; no one wants to climb on a roof or up a ladder if they don’t have to. We took all this into account during our tests, and the result is the following list of the best solar gutter lights for the job.

Bottom line: Solar gutter lights offer an easy, cost-effective way to enhance home security and style. UniqueFire stands out as the best overall choice.

To test the best solar gutter lights, we installed each light and took note of how easy or difficult the assembly and installation process was. We recorded the charging time for each and whether the lights performed well on sunny days, cloudy days and after a rainstorm. We noted how bright the lights were and if there were any additional features, such as motion detection or the ability to pivot or adjust the lights. The lights were left up for 2 weeks, including during a heavy summer rainstorm.

Each tested solar gutter light was evaluated on a scale of 1 to 5 across multiple categories: setup, appearance, light quality, durability, and value. We compiled the totals to get the rating for each category and ranked the solar gutter lights accordingly.

Before shopping for the best solar lights, there are some points to consider. Below are some of the factors that go into choosing the best solar gutter lights to help you decide which type is best for your specific application.

Note: These kinds of lights run independently of solar roof lights, a solar power system, or solar generator, so they don’t require any hardwiring or complicated installation.

Similar to solar garden path lights, the best solar gutter lights come in a wide range of brightness levels. Your lighting needs will determine which product is best for you. Many small clip-on lights offer just enough accent lighting to add a tasteful glow to your property. These lights provide between 20 and 50 lumens each, which is enough to illuminate a garden bed or a bit of a walkway relatively well.

For more light, there are models available with outputs over 500 lumens. These lights are excellent for lighting a driveway, fence line, or other areas you’d prefer to keep brightly lit.

Since most solar gutter lights attach directly to a home’s gutters, the materials chosen are an important factor. A light made with bulky materials, such as heavy-duty metal, will eventually bend and deform a gutter, so heft is worth considering.

By and large, the best solar gutter lights are made of plastic. These lights are lightweight but durable enough to withstand the elements. However, the brackets used to clip them to the gutter are usually steel, which gives these units the strength they need to withstand wind and heavy rains. Some of the lights that attach directly to the home’s structure might be aluminum, which is a more corrosion-resistant material than steel, and it’s also lighter weight.

Another important consideration is the IP rating. An IP rating (or Ingress Protection rating) indicates how well a light can stand up to elements like dust and water. The first number indicates how dustproof a light is on a scale of 1 to 5. The second number is water resistance. A number between 1 and 6 indicates a product is water-resistant, and 7 or 8 means it’s waterproof. Most of the lights on this list are either a 5 or 6 for being dustproof, and although they are all water-resistant, none are waterproof. Because these lights are charged by the rays of the sun, keeping them dust-free and keeping your gutters clean will directly influence the effectiveness of these lights.

It’s also important to note that while many of the lights claim to work at least 8 hours after a day of charging, cold weather can affect how well they stay charged. Therefore, these lights may perform for shorter periods, closer to 6 hours, when used during the winter or in cooler climates.

Most of the best solar gutter lights will automatically turn on when their built-in photosensors recognize that it’s getting dark. The length of time they run for, or their operating time, will vary depending on battery size, light output, and how much sun each light receives during a given day. Most of the lights we tested required 6 to 8 hours of charging time to last an average of 8 hours in the night, with some able to run as long as 10 to 12 hours.

Solar gutter lights have onboard batteries that charge using energy from the sun, similar to those found on solar chargers. The light absorbs solar energy via a built-in photovoltaic cell. The cell then converts the energy into electricity and stores it in the battery. For some of the lights, the battery is a built-in component, but others take a rechargeable AA battery. This battery is most often included with the lights and may need to be replaced every 12 months to 3 years, depending on manufacturer’s recommendation and how much weather the lights have endured.

Battery power output can vary between 800 and up to 3,000 milliamp hours, and the larger the battery, the more energy it can produce. The panel’s size relative to the battery’s size determines how efficiently the light will charge. Too large a cell and the battery will fill too quickly, wasting sunlight. Too small and a battery may never reach its full potential. For this reason, most manufacturers try to size their photovoltaic cells to match their output ratings.

Choosing the best solar gutter lights for your home might come down to ease of installation. Many of these models simply attach to the lip of a home’s gutters, tightening down onto the edge. All that’s required to secure them is a ladder and a pair of pliers or a screwdriver, depending on the model.

Other models might require the user to attach them directly to the home’s structure with brackets and screws. While this could seem like an inconvenience, these models typically have the greatest light output and battery life, so there is a trade-off. Installing these lights typically requires a ladder, a power drill, and a screwdriver.

In general, most solar lights are function first, meaning they may not add to a home’s curb appeal. But, there are models available that aren’t as jarring to the eye. For the most part, gutters on homes are white, so most gutter lights are available in white plastic. Homes with gutters in other colors might look better with black solar gutter lights, which are readily available.

If you’re unable to find a light that matches well with your home’s aesthetic, you can still achieve attractive outdoor lighting by finding a model that attaches directly to the home’s structure. This allows them to be hidden under the eave somewhat, but it’s important that they get at least some sunlight to function as expected.

Some additional features help increase the convenience and functionality of the best solar gutter lights. For example, a motion sensor might activate when it senses someone or something walking underneath it, which is excellent for security.

Many models also come with automatic switches that activate the light once a sensor determines it’s getting dark. And should the battery still have enough charge by morning, the controller will turn the light off when the sun comes up. There are also models with remote controls, which allow you to operate the lights remotely and adjust their output without climbing a ladder.

If you still have some questions about the best solar gutter lights, this section is for you. It’s a collection of some of the most frequently asked questions about solar gutter lights. Be sure to check for an answer to your question below.

Solar lights work best when the light is most available. While solar gutter lights are weatherproof and designed for year-round use, it’s important to remember that heavy snowfall can break and damage gutters, and also the lights.

Solar gutter lights typically come with everything necessary for setup and use.

There are solar lights that produce as much as 1,500 lumens of brightness.

Most solar lights are not motion activated, but there are solar lights that have motion-activated features.

If properly cared for, many solar gutter lights can last for years. Manufacturers frequently offer a 1-year warranty on gutter lights, but this can vary depending on the product, material, and type of weather the lights may endure.

#7827. One More Round of Winter Container Inspiration

Hi everyone! Before we jump in, a quick note: We had a little technical hiccup today, and our GPOD didn’t publish when it was supposed to. If you missed it, you can catch up on Ellen Goldfarb and Tracy Buttrick’s winter container designs here.

Now, let’s finish out the week with one more round of winter inspiration from Ellen and Tracy of What’s Blooming! I hope these containers have given you plenty of ideas to play around with in your own seasonal displays.

This cedar-shake square pot in Tenafly, New Jersey, is one of a pair flanking the steps of this rustic porch. It is under the roof, so the artificial cardinals won’t disintegrate! For height, we used birch logs, some short stems of curly willow, and lots of silver bell eucalyptus.

The greens were desert juniper (Juniperus osteosperma, Zones 3–9), noble fir (Abies procera, Zones 5–6), and incense cedar (Calocedrus decurrens, Zones 5–8). Pine cones, both frosted and brown, and small bunches of silver brunia finished off the planter.

Close-up of a tall, stand-alone pot out in front of a house in Allendale, New Jersey: It can be seen from all sides. We used tall birch logs and tall stems of heavily berried Chinese juniper (Juniperus chinensis, Zones 4–9). Silver bell eucalyptus, small curly willow branches, frosted pine cones, silver brunia clusters, and incense cedar branches fill out the arrangement.

The owner of this house in Saddle River just loved red winterberries (Ilex verticillata, Zones 3–9), so we used lots of them! There was plenty of room for height, so we added tall curly willow, which contrasted nicely with the white background.

There are some tall Chinese juniper tucked in and rosettes of magnolia leaves with natural brown pine cones, silver brunia clusters, a little noble fir, and lots of incense cedar around the rim.

Here you can see the previous planter on the front porch with its partner.

Thanks so much to Ellen and Tracy for sharing this incredible collection of winter containers with us! Please continue to submit images of all the beautiful containers you create. I can only imagine what spring and summer look like!

Hopefully everyone found a new combination, material, or idea to try in their own containers this winter. Have a wonderful weekend, and we’ll see you back here on Monday!

Peace lilies may be entering a slower growth phase, but a few quick checks can make or break the healthy and vitality of your favorite houseplants over winter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Your peace lily (Spathiphyllum) may well have spent the early part of fall thriving in its regular corner with little more than a weekly drink. But this can all change sharply when November arrives. Suddenly, the lower leaves droop, that trademark glossy sheen can look dull, and the leaf tips might turn dry and brown, even if you haven't changed your routine. The real shift is taking place in the house around the plant, and that’s easy to miss when the plant hasn’t moved an inch.

Peace lilies are naturally resilient, but they are sensitive to environmental shifts. The days are shorter, the sunlight angles have dropped, and central heating systems are kicking into gear. Good peace lily care through winter is largely about keeping up with those changes. The good news is that the fixes are small. It’s just about recognizing that your plant’s needs change as winter starts to set in.

By tweaking your habits and pausing unnecessary chores that may have been essential just a month earlier, you can protect root health and ensure your peace lily remains a centerpiece of lush green calm throughout these next few chilly months. Not only will these adjustments protect your favorite houseplant in winter, they will help to set the stage for more striking white spathes come spring. So here’s how to keep your peace lily healthy once the heat comes on…

Indoor winter living often creates conditions that clash with tropical houseplant health. We seal our doors, turn up the furnace, and seek out cozy, dry warmth. For a peace lily, that same forced-air heating strips ambient room humidity down to single digits while leaving drafty windowpanes ice-cold. Coexisting happily indoors through winter means balancing these conditions, providing the warmth your peace lily needs while protecting it against parched air, dark corners, and soggy soil.

Diagnosing leaf symptoms early in November prevents minor seasonal stress from escalating into root damage. If your entire plant suddenly collapses into a limp heap, check the soil before reaching for the watering can. If the potting mix is bone dry, a thorough drink will perk the foliage up within hours. If the mix feels soggy and heavy while the leaves hang limp, waterlogged roots are suffocating: stop watering now!

Brown, crispy leaf tips usually stem from low humidity, uneven moisture, or mineral salt accumulation from tap water. Occasional yellowing on a leaf lower down is normal ageing. However, multiple yellow leaves can indicate insufficient light or waterlogged compost or insufficient light. A long-probe soil moisture meter can help you determine deeper root moisture. I’m a big fan of the XLUX Long Probe Soil Moisture Meter, available from Amazon, which delivers instant readings, so you can address overwatering and soggy potting mix before fungal rot sets in.

As for flowers, don't expect too many right now. Winter usually isn't when peace lilies bloom. A plant that rarely flowers at all, though, probably needs a brighter spot, unless it's still young (under a year old, some won't bloom yet). Knowing some of the warning signs, hopefully the following tasks will help you avoid calamity this winter…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The quickest way to harm a peace lily in November is sticking to a rigid summer watering schedule. As natural day length shortens and light intensity wanes, your plant enters a semi-dormant rest period. Transpiration slows, cell division halts, and roots need less moisture from the soil. A potting blend that dried out in 5 days during July can easily stay damp for 3 weeks in November. Keeping the soil constantly saturated starves roots of oxygen, eventually leading to Pythium root rot.

This step is easy: insert a finger a couple of inches (5cm) into the potting mix. Water only when it feels dry and crumbly to the touch. When you do water your peace lily, soak the root ball thoroughly with room-temperature water until it drains freely from the base, then empty any runoff collected in the saucer. Never leave a peace lily sitting in stagnant, chilled water. If your plant droops, check soil dampness first.

A nifty way of reducing the risks associated with poor drainage is to give your plants some elevation in the drainage tray. Kakuna Plant Pot Feet, available from Amazon, can be inserted between the pot and tray to minimize chills and waterlogging.

Peace lilies have an enduring reputation as indestructible low-light houseplants, but there is a difference between surviving and thriving. While they tolerate the subdued light of a shaded summer room, the dramatic drop in November’s daylight hours and sun intensity can throw low-light corners into near-darkness. Without help, your peace lily cannot produce the energy needed to support its broad leaf surface, leading to faded foliage, drooping stems, and a halt in flower spathe production.

Take time now to reassess where your peace lily sits and check how much light reaches the plant around noon. If needed, move the plant closer to an east or north-facing window, where it can absorb hours of bright, indirect winter daylight. Keep the leaves a few inches (8-10cm) back from direct contact with windowpanes, as freezing outdoor temperatures radiate through cold glass and will chill leaf tissue.

If placing your plant near a south or west-facing window where bright afternoon sun beams through, hang a sheer curtain to diffuse the rays; direct, unfiltered sunlight can still scorch foliage even in winter. For darker rooms lacking bright exposures, supplemental artificial light provides an easy fix. The GE BR30 Grow LED Light Bulb from Walmart fits a standard socket and lamp fixture, emitting balanced, warm-toned full-spectrum light that sustains photosynthesis through dark winter months.

Indoor central heating is a double hazard for peace lilies: it strips moisture from the air, while creating extreme temperature pockets. Peace lilies thrive in relative humidity levels between 50% and 60%. When heating systems get switched on, indoor humidity frequently plunges below 20%. This dry air saps moisture from leaf margins, causing crispy brown edges and papery tips. Position your plant away from forced-air vents, radiators, space heaters, and wood stoves. The blast of hot air will quickly scorch foliage. At the same time, keep plants shielded from exterior door drafts and chilly single-pane windows, maintaining a range of 65-80°F (18-27°C).

Skip leaf misting, which provides only a brief humidity spike and can encourage fungal leaf spotting. Instead, place your pot on a wide tray filled with pebbles and water (keeping the pot base resting above the water line). Alternatively, group multiple houseplants together, or run a small ultrasonic room humidifier nearby. To help you track things, buy a digital sensor like the TempPro TP50 Digital Room Temperature and Humidity Monitor, available from The Home Depot. This compact digital sensor monitors relative humidity and ambient temperature fluctuations, helping you pinpoint cold drafts and heating hotspots.

During the dark days of late fall and winter, feeding a peace lily does far more harm than good. Because diminished daylight slows metabolic activity, the plant is not producing new tissue or developing roots. Adding liquid houseplant fertilizer during this semi-dormant time means mineral salts can build up in the potting soil. Over several weeks, this salt buildup can burn roots and brown leaf tips. Now is the time to withhold all supplemental feeding until active spring growth returns in late March.

Similarly, postpone repotting until the warmer, brighter days of spring. It doesn’t matter if you see a few roots poking out of the drainage holes: peace lilies tolerate being slightly pot-bound and recover faster in spring. Moving a sluggish plant into a larger pot now can shock them. The only exception is emergency repotting. If a plant has collapsed from severe root rot, gently tip it from its pot and rinse away old soil. Trim off brown mushy roots with sterile shears, and repot into fresh, well-aerated potting mix. A great lightweight blend for emergency winter repotting is Espoma Organic Houseplant Potting Soil Mix, available at The Home Depot.

In just a few weeks, broad peace lily leaves collect a fine film of household dust, pet dander, and airborne grease. Dusty foliage can be severely limiting in winter. Dust acts as a barrier, scattering what little winter light reaches the leaves and reducing the plant's already limited photosynthetic capacity. Cleaning the foliage is a quick, high-reward task that keeps leaves breathing and photosynthesizing efficiently. Support each leaf from beneath with one hand, and gently wipe the upper and lower surfaces with a soft cloth moistened with room-temperature water.

As you clean, inspect the leaf undersides and stem junctions for pests. Dry winter heating can encourage rapid outbreaks unless you catch them early. Bits of white fluff could be citrus mealybugs (Planococcus citri). Flat tan bumps are often brown soft scale (Coccus hesperidum). Faint speckling and webbing usually mean twospotted spider mites (Tetranychus urticae), which thrive in dry, heated rooms. Gently dab mealybug clusters with a cotton swab dipped in rubbing alcohol, or treat leaf undersides with a gentle organic insecticidal soap or neem oil wash. Bonide Captain Jack’s Neem Oil Spray, available from Amazon, is a brilliant organic way of controlling spider mites, scale, and mealybugs.

By giving your peace lily a little focused attention in November, you provide the support it needs to navigate the winter months with ease. Dialing back the watering can, finding a brighter pocket of filtered daylight, raising ambient moisture levels, and letting the roots rest will keep the foliage healthy and glossy.

Set up well in November, a peace lily usually comes through winter looking much like it did in summer, just growing a little slower. The fertilizer and the bigger pot can wait until spring, and so can you. When longer spring days return, your well-rested peace lily will be primed to surge back into active growth, rewarding you with fresh green leaves and a striking display of signature white blooms.

With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7825. The Best Space Heaters of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Stacey L. Nash, Tom Scalisi, Additional research provided by Glenda Taylor

Published Nov 6, 2026 9:30 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Ever-rising utility costs can make heating an entire house prohibitively pricey, so to save money but still keep occupied areas comfortable, many renters and homeowners take advantage of space heaters. Today’s models offer basic heating features at more affordable prices, convenient bells and whistles, and upgraded safety features. To help you choose the model with the aspects you want most, we put 11 space heaters through a series of hands-on tests.

Testing took place in real-life scenarios to put performance and safety features on the spot and to give us an inside look at how each model functioned over time. We also spoke to Robin Saidov, an energy industry expert, electrical engineer, and the owner of Your Energy Footprint, a company in Westport, Connecticut, that educates consumers on ways to be more energy efficient. Based on our tests and Robin’s advice, we chose the Amazon Basics Portable Manual-Control Radiator Heater as our top pick for its easy assembly, noiseless operation, and ample heat. Below, learn what we found, how to navigate the options, and why the models below are among the best space heaters available.

Bottom line: Space heaters offer cost-effective warmth with enhanced safety features. Choose the right model based on room size and energy efficiency for the best results.

A space heater can be a welcome source of supplemental warmth in a chilly room, especially if it also saves money on utility costs by allowing the user to turn the HVAC thermostat down a few degrees. Keep in mind that space heaters get very hot and, if used carelessly, they can lead to a house fire. Before looking for a space heater, it’s a good idea for shoppers to call their homeowners insurance agent, since some insurance policies will not cover damages from a fire caused by a space heater.

To qualify as a top pick, a space heater needed to show in our testing that it was powerful enough to heat the intended room. We also made sure each included safety features that would turn the unit off if it fell over. The following models are suited to various heating needs, and any one of them might well serve a variety of situations.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Performance 3/5; Noise 5/5; Portability 4/5; Value 4/5

The Amazon Basics portable manual-control radiator heater is aptly named, as it is a basic space heater. This oil-filled radiator features two control knobs (temperature and output) for setting the heater and letting it do its work, so it is very easy to use.

This model features a 1,500W output, allowing it to heat large rooms. It also features a tip-over switch and overheat protection for safety, and it operates nearly silently, aside from the sound of an air bubble in the oil now and then. It measures 26.38 inches tall (with wheels) by 13.19 inches wide by 9.84 inches deep. It features a top-mounted handle for transport as well, and it weighs 15.41 pounds.

There isn’t a lot to say about the Amazon Basics oil heater. It was easy to assemble and use, and it produced plenty of heat (although it took 2 hours to heat a living room from 60 to 70 degrees Fahrenheit). There isn’t a digital display or remote control to adjust the temperature, but the fact that it provides silent heat is really a plus—all that’s discernible is a click every now and then when the heating element kicks on and off. It might be a little too simple for tech lovers, however.

Get the Amazon Basics space heater at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Performance 4/5; Noise 3/5; Portability 5/5; Value 5/5

For a reasonable price, this oscillating heater provides 1,500 watts of heat, enough to keep a 150-square-foot room warm and cozy. It features three power outputs (low, high, and fan only), plus tip-over shutoff for safety should it inadvertently get knocked over. There’s a simple on/off switch for easy operation and a thermostat dial that allows the user to select the desired temperature. After the user sets the thermostat, the heater will turn itself on and off to maintain the selected temperature. It weighs a mere 3.2 pounds and boasts a handle on the back for easy toting from room to room.

While this simple heater did well during testing, it doesn’t have any features that make it stand out. The basic heat functions worked well, and the adjustable thermostat triggered an automatic shutoff. However, it could use a display to show the exact temperature setting. The current variable thermostat left us guessing as to the temperature we were choosing. Overall, it’s lightweight, portable, and made quick work of heating a 150-square-foot office.

Get the Amazon Basics oscillating space heater at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Performance 4/5; Noise 3/5; Portability 3/5; Value 4/5

For warmth and peace of mind, consider the ample safety features of the AirNmore Comfort Deluxe infrared space heater. Though it will heat a room up to 150 square feet, its outer casing will remain cool to the touch, which is crucial for homes with kids and pets. The tip-over safety function shuts the unit off if it gets knocked over, but since it weighs 22 pounds, this is a less likely scenario than with some smaller models. A 14-gauge cord with a three-prong heater plug reduces the risk of the cord melting from overheating.

The power level is adjustable, and the heater has a built-in thermostat to maintain a consistent temperature. A removable, washable filter prevents dust from recirculating in the air. Users might mistake this space heater for an old-time radio; it definitely looks more design-friendly than some other more utilitarian models. We loved this heater in testing, although with infrared heaters, users have to direct the heat toward themselves. It’s a penetrating heat, but only if it hits the body.

A tiny remote control let us change modes (low or high) and temperatures while working at a desk, and we liked that we could precisely adjust the temperature setting and see it on the display. The downside with this AirNmore space heater is its size. It’s big and takes up a lot of room while heating up a relatively small 150-square-foot space. However, the casters make moving this behemoth out of the way when not in use fairly easy.

Get the AirNmore space heater at Amazon or Walmart.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Performance 5/5; Noise 5/5; Portability 4/5; Value 5/5

This electric heater from Lasko’s Designer series has smooth contours and rests on an attractive base so that it looks more like a work of art than a space heater. Appearance aside, the ceramic model effectively heats rooms up to 150 square feet by oscillating smoothly from side to side for uniform heat distribution. Switch between its adjustable heat settings via the remote; the Lasko can even be programmed in advance to turn on and off when desired. This handsome space heater also features a safety shutoff in case the unit tips over.

This beauty was a pleasant surprise during testing because it cranks out the heat. It might be designed to heat 150-square-foot spaces, but it can do more than that with the heat it puts out. The oscillating setting spread the heat far and wide, quickly warming our 200-square-foot test space (another office) to perfection. We liked that we could pick the temperature setting, though it only goes in 5 degree Fahrenheit increments. Plus, it comes with a timer that automatically turns the unit off after 1, 2, or 4 hours. With that set, we didn’t worry about leaving it on while we were away.

Once the room reaches the set temperature, this space heater automatically shuts off. However, we noticed that if the temperature began to fall, it didn’t automatically turn back on. But we could turn it back on using the remote, so no one actually had to get out of their chair. This model might have made us a little lazy.

Get the Lasko space heater at Amazon or Best Buy.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Performance 5/5; Noise 5/5; Portability 3/5; Value 4/5

This 1,500-watt portable space heater from Dr. Infrared Heater looks like a classic radio but runs like the high-tech space heater that it is. Emitting only 39 decibels, this infrared heater features quiet air circulation that moves the heat through large spaces. We tested it in a 200-square-foot office, and this space heater made quick work of warming it. Infrared heaters don’t heat the air; instead, they heat objects. This heater’s quiet fan made it feel like the heat permeated farther and made a difference in overall room temperature.

It’s also packed with features including standby, eco, low, and high power modes. The digital display shows the thermostat’s setting, which makes it easy to make adjustments based on comfort levels.

We’re big fans of remote controls. This model’s remote control allowed us to make comfort adjustments without getting out of our office chair. We appreciated that we could leave it on all day while we worked, and it would turn on and off as needed. There’s also an adjustable timer, which can go up to 12 hours before automatically shutting off the heater.

Overall, it’s a nice-looking heater that can handle spaces up to about 850 square feet. It’s not the most mobile unit, weighing 24 pounds, but it does have casters for easier mobility.

Get the Dr. Infrared Heater space heater at Amazon, Lowe’s, The Home Depot, Walmart, or Dr. Heater.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 4/5; Performance 4/5; Noise 5/5; Portability 5/5; Value 4/5

Figuring out the heat in a finished basement can be an ordeal but might be easily solved with the De’Longhi SlimStyle digital convection panel heater. This model can be set on the floor or mounted on the wall (the latter being best for basement duty), and it produces up to 1,500 watts of heating power. It measures 21.8 inches tall (with feet) by 32.2 inches wide by 8.5 inches deep.

The De’Longhi features a convection-style design that is virtually silent in three out of the four modes, and a fourth mode with a fan to help pump out the heat. It also features a fifth mode (anti-freeze), which the manufacturer says kicks on when the temperature in the space reaches 41 degrees Fahrenheit; this is to help prevent frozen pipes. The heater has a built-in tip-over switch as well as an overheat sensor, timers, and an electronic digital display. Unfortunately, it doesn’t come with a remote.

We’re not relegating the De’Longhi to the basement because it’s ugly; we honestly found it very nice looking. However, we think it’s best there for its included wall-mount brackets and the fact that it has a freeze-protection mode (ours activated at 45 degrees, not 41 like the manufacturer stated). With so many pipes and mechanicals in a finished basement, we thought this was the perfect solution to protect the investment. Also, most space heaters don’t reach settings that low, so this one works really well for that purpose.

There is one thing we couldn’t figure out, however: Why in the world doesn’t it come with a remote?

Get the De’Longhi SlimStyle space heater at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Ease of Use 5/5; Performance 5/5; Noise 5/5; Portability 4/5; Value 4/5

The Heat Storm Logan Deluxe infrared heater is all about coziness. This powerful space heater features a 1,500W output, a digital display, and a remote control for managing the device from the couch. It has a faux-wood box-style design with fabric-covered sides, allowing it to blend in with comfortable living room decor. It can also handle large living rooms, considering it can warm up to 1,000 square feet.

This model features several modes—including high, medium, low, and auto—that control the heater based on the preset temperature. It also has a safe-touch exterior that remains cool and safe, a child lock, and overheat protection. The heater operates quietly (measured at 46 decibels on a sound meter app from about 4 feet away) as well. It measures 15.3 inches tall (with wheels) by 12.3 inches wide by 10.8 inches deep.

We’ll be honest and say that this heater has to match a living room decor to be a perfect fit, but if one of the three finish color options works, the unit can sit in the corner of any room and blend in until it’s needed.

While it’s light (10 pounds), the box itself is simply faux wood, which doesn’t seem as high in quality as other real-wood heaters that we’ve tested in the past. It had a better digital display than any of those other box-style heaters, however, and it produced a lot of heat, bringing a 63 degree Fahrenheit living room to 70 degrees Fahrenheit in about 15 minutes. Also, for those who care, it blows hot air out at the perfect height for one of our old dogs, who instantly laid down in front of it and fell asleep. We assume other four-legged friends will love it, too.

Get the Heat Storm Logan space heater at Amazon.

This space heater performed well in many respects. It has an adjustable thermostat, 11 heat settings, a cool-touch exterior, and a compact design. What it doesn’t have is an automatic tilt shut-off feature. That means if it gets knocked over, it keeps running. In a home with pets, kids, and, honestly, most adults, it could keep running face down, posing a fire hazard. For that reason, it didn’t make our list of top picks.

We tested these space heaters in person, in real-world situations. They were all tested in a home office setting where the office was 150 to 200 square feet in size. One of the test offices also had large windows, so the room temperature fluctuated more often. We tried them on different surfaces, from plush carpet to bare floors.

For models with a digital display, we set the thermostat between 70 and 75 degrees Fahrenheit to see how well the space heater kept a consistent room temperature. From there, we made adjustments to settings (low and high), timers, and safety features. For example, we tipped over every single space heater to make sure it turned off.

Models designed to turn on and off based on the thermostat were left running to see how they performed over time. Some stayed in standby mode for hours without turning on because a furnace kept the room at temperature. We wanted to make sure they wouldn’t turn on if it wasn’t necessary. Ease of use was also a consideration, and models with remote controls or intuitive designs got higher marks from us.

Besides taking into account the size of the room you’re planning to heat, Saidov says it’s a good idea to “find a model that has a set temperature.” She adds, “This will ensure that the unit doesn’t overheat the space.” She also says to make sure the space heater is Underwriters Laboratories (UL) certified, a third-party certification that means the heater meets certain safety standards. And, most importantly, “Electric space heaters should always be plugged into a wall outlet and grounded. Using extension cords and power strips can be a fire hazard.”

A small space heater might be suitable under a desk or next to a lounge chair, but it likely won’t make a dent in a sizable chilly room. A space heater’s size should suit the room that it will warm and should, of course, be as safe as possible.

For those just starting to shop, it might come as a surprise to find so many different types of heaters from which to choose. Each type has its pros and cons, and not all space heaters are suitable for all rooms and situations.

Fan space heaters function by heating the air around an electric coil or wire elements and then dispersing the heat with a fan. They are among the least expensive models but do not offer the same efficiency as other types. Therefore, fan heaters are best suited to rooms without drafts or for warming a small space quickly.

Convection space heaters warm air over ceramic plates or disks and allow it to radiate warmth into the room. Some models do include fans for quicker heat dispersal and, like conventional fan heaters, they work best in rooms without drafts. Convection heaters come in compact or tower models, often with exterior cases that are cooler to the touch. Prices vary depending on wattage and added features.

Infrared space heaters are among the quietest options for the home. They generate heat quickly by radiating heat to the objects—including people—in front of them. As opposed to heating the air in the room, this type of heater heats the user, making it a good choice for use in drafty rooms. All that’s needed is for the user to aim it directly at where they’re sitting.

Oil-filled space heaters (another type of radiant heater) are also a quiet option. Because they are capable of putting off an abundance of heat while using less electricity than fan-type models, these heaters are well suited to larger rooms. Due to the weight of the oil and the steel casing, these heaters are relatively heavy, but many come with wheels to make relocating easier. Oil-filled space heaters take a while to heat up, but they radiate continuously once they do.

Micathermic space heaters combine convection and radiant heating processes. Designed as a panel to stand or hang on a wall like a piece of artwork, they create a welcoming ambience for the senses by mimicking the look of a real fire and radiating heat. Some models include fans for greater efficiency and remote controls for extra convenience. These advanced heaters vary widely in price.

Space heaters are a leading cause of house fires, so the best space heaters boast safety features to reduce risk. Manufacturers have introduced automatic shutoffs that kick in when a unit overheats or gets inadvertently knocked over. In addition, many have exterior cases that keep units cool to the touch at all times. Some models even come equipped with motion sensors that automatically turn the heater off when a pet or child comes too close. For extra peace of mind when purchasing, look for the letters NRTL on the space heater packaging, which indicates that the model has been tested for safety by the Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratory.

As a general rule of thumb, select a space heater that will produce 10 watts of power for every square foot. For instance, to heat a 12-foot-long by 10-foot-wide room, a shopper would need to purchase a 1,200W space heater. A very large room may require more than one space heater to maintain a comfortable temperature throughout.

Other factors that affect a space heater’s efficiency include ceiling height, the insulating factor of the exterior walls, the number of windows, and the available outlets. While high-wattage heaters offer more heat than lower-wattage models, they’re limited to the capacity of the electrical outlet; a home’s standard 110-volt electrical outlet can only provide 1,500W of power, so that must be the wattage cap for any machine plugged into it.

One of the main reasons for using a space heater is to save on energy costs. But unlike many other appliances, space heaters do not require energy testing by the Environmental Protection Agency, nor does the agency issue Energy Star ratings for them, so those who are serious about saving will want to opt for the most efficient type.

Oil-filled space heaters are among the most efficient because they heat the oil and the metal casing, gradually dispersing radiant warmth into the room. Once the oil reaches the desired temperature, less energy is needed to maintain that temperature. Even after an oil-filled heater is turned off, it will continue to radiate heat for up to 30 minutes or more. Next in energy efficiency are infrared space heaters, which use up to 10 percent less energy than space heaters with coils and fans.

For the most part, space heaters are among the quietest of all small appliances. Space heaters that use radiant heat, either infrared or oil-filled, make virtually no noise. Traditional space heaters with fans will emit an average of 35 to 45 decibels of sound, approximately the same as soft indoor conversation (which could be suitable to use as a white noise machine).

Homeowners and renters can save on utility costs by using a space heater in one or more rooms rather than heating the entire home. For the toastiest—and safest—results, check out these useful tips.

Most space heaters should be turned off at night and when you leave a room. The exception is an oil-filled radiating space heater, which can be left on. However, make certain not to leave anything flammable within 3 feet of the radiator.

Oil-filled radiant heaters use the least amount of electricity because once they heat up, it takes very little energy to keep them warm. Plus, they will radiate heat for up to 30 minutes or more after they’ve been turned off.

The safest space heater is one that will automatically shut off if it overheats or if it accidentally tips over.

#7824. The Clever Way to Reuse Old Tomato Cages to Protect Your Plants From Freezing Temperatures

Your empty tomato cages can shelter tender shrubs from frost and snow all winter and help safeguard next summer's flowers.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Wrapped in frost cloth or burlap, an old tomato cage becomes a cheap but effective shelter to protect plants this winter. All sorts of tender shrubs and perennials need winter protection, and temporarily shielding even hardy plants from the worst of the weather can help them thrive. So if you're about to pack away your tomato cages in the shed, stop – they've got another job to do now it's time to winterize garden plants this fall.

Pulling up tomato plants and stacking their cages in the shed until spring is one of the last big gardening jobs of the season. That's a lot of good wire sitting around in the dark all winter, and this trick puts it right back to work. Most gardens have a plant or two that struggles through the cold months, and overwintering plants usually means spending money on shrub covers, frost tents or frames, or insulating zip-up plant jackets built for the job. None of it costs much alone, but the outlay adds up across a whole bed and your old cage can do much of that same work to winterize plants.

This trick won't save everything, but for the right plants a tomato cage wrapped in frost cloth or burlap is a smart, cheap way to help your garden get through winter unscathed. So, if you're gardening on a budget and wondering how to protect plants in winter, here's the smart solution.

Throw insulating fabric straight over a shrub and it settles right onto the leaves and buds, and cold will seep through wherever it touches. Wet snow is worse. Its weight can bend or snap branches under the cover. But put a tomato cage in there first and the fabric sits on the frame instead, with a little gap between cover and plant. This method also gives you a frame to fasten the fabric to so it stays put when the wind picks up.

Start with the cage itself. You'll probably find dried leaves and sections of vine still wound through the wire. If last summer's plants had Septoria leaf spot (Septoria lycopersici) or early blight (Alternaria solani), those scraps can carry it over, so pull every one out and disinfect by scrubbing the cage with diluted household bleach and a rinse.

Next comes the fit. Lower the clean cage over the plant and see where the branches end up. Any branch poking through the wire is, more or less, where the fabric will touch the plant later, so the stems need room inside. Push the legs down firmly and, out in an open, windy bed, tie it to a sturdy stake if needs be.

Now wrap the frame in breathable frost cloth or horticultural fleece: one Agfabric frost blanket, available from Home Depot, covers more than one cage. Fasten the fabric to the frame using clips like these stainless steel garden clips from Walmart. Take the fabric right down to the soil as warmth comes up out of the ground at night and a gap at the bottom lets it leak out. Pin the fabric to the ground with galvanized landscape staples like these from Walmart.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Skip plastic wrap, because the plant needs to breathe and a wrapped cage heats up fast on mild afternoons and damp, still air favors gray mold (Botrytis cinerea). Even without a waterproof wrap, peek underneath every few days and let some fresh air in if needs be. Once the cold snap is over, take the temporary covers off, leaving the frame in place ready for the next weather dip.

Depending on your USDA zone, the plants that need winterizing in fall aren't just those that aren't hardy enough to survive plummeting temperatures: you can use this trick to extend a crop or protect next year's flower show, too. Ever had a hydrangea leaf out nicely and then barely bloom? Bigleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea macrophylla) is the classic candidate because it forms next year's flower buds on old wood, and those buds sit on bare stems all winter. Hard freezes can kill these delicate buds so while the foliage comes through just fine the following year, blooms are few and far between.

Hybrid tea roses and perennials that are borderline hardy in your zone are good candidates too. If you've planted young shrubs this year – especially if you've been tempted by Black Friday sales on evergreen shrubs and you're planting late in fall – they'll also benefit from being kept cozy during cold snaps. Boxwood and other small evergreens can pick up winter burn from drying wind and sun, and burlap like this Wellco natural burlap roll at Home Depotcuts down on both without pressing on the foliage.

Of course, you'll need to match the plant to the cage size. But if you're planning to upgrade your tomato cages to use a more substantial modular tomato support set-up like these heavy-duty square tomato cages, also from Home Depot anyway, it makes sense to do so now when you can use them to protect bigger shrubs that need a wider frame.

Once the plant goes dormant, usually after several hard frosts, a sturdy cage can be packed with loose insulation to provide further insulation too. Dry shredded leaves, straw or pine straw like this from Amazon is best. On a bigleaf hydrangea, you can fill right up around the buds, while roses mostly need the extra insulation over the crown and lower canes.

Keep that fill dry and loose. Leaves raked off a wet lawn and packed tight against living foliage or a crown stay soggy, and that can lead to rot, so let them dry out first before covering with frost fabric. In spring, pull out the fill a little at a time once the worst cold has passed.

Frost cloth doesn't make any heat of its own, but only slows the loss of warmth rising from the ground at night, buying a few degrees on a clear, still night. In a long, deep freeze, the soil underneath cools off too, and that leaves the cover less and less to work with. Truly tropical plants won't turn winter-hardy inside a wrapped cage, either: hibiscus and mandevilla belong indoors once nights turn chilly, well ahead of frost. In colder regions, some tender plants on the edge of hardiness still do better potted up and stored in a frost-free spot.

For most of the year, a tomato cage has one job. But with a cozy comforter of frost cloth, a few clips and a bit of care, this garden staple picks up a second role in winter, sheltering plants that would otherwise need a store-bought cover and helping to ensure another flower-filled year in your garden. When spring comes, unwrap your precious plant, hose off the cage and send it back to the tomato bed. It's the same old cage pulling double duty, and this trick to reuse it over winter barely costs a dime.

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#7823. 8 Things I Learned About Gardening From an Amish Farmer – and Why They're Worth Trying in Your Own Yard

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

Some of this Amish farmer's gardening wisdom might sound old-fashioned, but his practical advice has plenty to teach modern gardeners.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Some of the best gardening tips never make it onto a seed packet. They come from people who've worked the same ground for years and notice what the rest of us walk past – like how a tomato leaf changes color before trouble starts.

I recently stumbled across a fascinating piece of gardening history that feels just as relevant today as it did when it was written. Back in 2013, Amish farmer Joni Miller sent Modern Farmer a 45-page handwritten essay on organic gardening and farming, packed with diagrams and advice on everything from compost to certification paperwork. All he asked in return was a two-year subscription.

Much of what Miller wrote will sound familiar to organic growers. Some of it surprised me, though, and it's fascinating to see how well his ideas line up with newer research. These are the eight lessons I found most interesting, and how to use each one at home.

Miller suggests making a little chart of leaf colors, and I love the idea of reading a vegetable bed that way. For tomatoes and eggplant, he says lower leaves that yellow once the plants start bearing give up their potassium to the fruit. A black, rotting spot on a tomato's bottom – aka blossom-end rot – in his experience, means poor calcium uptake.

Newer research largely agrees, though each symptom has other causes, too. Lower leaves also yellow from a nitrogen shortage, plain old age, or early blight (Alternaria linariae). Blossom-end rot does come from calcium not reaching the fruit, but the soil usually has plenty, and uneven watering tends to be the real trouble. I'd sort that out before buying fertilizer.

The weed section grabbed me most. Miller noticed foxtail and other grassy weeds sprouting better in tight, high-magnesium soils, and lambsquarters surging after heavy turkey manure. Velvetleaf liked rich ground, Canada thistle faded once soil was loose and cultivated, and pastures full of dandelions never grew lush. As he puts it, "Reading soils by their weeds is an art!"

Researchers read weeds the same way today, as clues with wiggle room. Weeds tolerate a range of conditions, so dandelions might mean compacted soil and chickweed might mean wet ground, or a neighbor's seed heads might just be blowing your way. Then confirm with a soil test, using a home kit that you send to a lab, like the MySoil Soil Test Kit, available on Amazon.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Miller's pest advice starts with life cycles, using squash bugs (Anasa tristis) as his example. The nymphs that hatch look like little spiders and start out soft. Each molt hardens them, and by the later ones, he found few organic sprays could touch them. If oil can't smother the eggs, his trick is to "target for those young spiderlings while they're easier prey."

That means turning squash leaves over. Look at the undersides, often in the crook between two veins, and you'll spot copper-brown egg clusters. Duct tape pulls them off easily. If a few nymphs get past you, insecticidal soap or neem oil, like Bonide Captain Jack's Neem Oil Spray, will knock them back, sprayed early or late, when bees are quieter. Adults, by then, are another story, and hand-picking works better on them.

Straw mulch is nothing new, so Miller's note about greenhouse tomato growers using alfalfa hay caught my attention. It keeps weeds down, but the bigger benefit, he says, is that "the decomposing alfalfa feeds the vegetables with high-quality nutrients."

Modern studies hold that up. Alfalfa is a legume, so it has more nitrogen than straw and breaks down faster. It holds moisture, too. Once the soil warms, spread 2–3 inches (5–8 cm) of weed-free hay around tomatoes and peppers, leaving a gap at the stems.

Ask if the hay field was sprayed, as some hay herbicides linger, and tomatoes are very sensitive. Can't find bales? Try using alfalfa meal instead, like Down to Earth organic alfalfa meal from Walmart.

I was surprised to learn you can time weeding with a thermometer. Miller counts heat units. You average each day's high and low, but a high over 90°F (32°C) only counts as 90, a low under 50°F (10°C) counts as 50, and you subtract 50. Weed seeds need about 60 units to germinate, he says, so he harrows right before that and starts back at zero with each new flush.

Weed researchers still study the same idea today, under the label stale seedbed, which is a funny name for it, honestly. Simply prepare the bed a few weeks early, water it, and wait for the first weeds, usually a week or two in warm soil. Slice them off in the top inch (2.5 cm) – digging deeper brings buried seeds up to sprout. WaLensee's stirrup-style action hoe from Home Depot suits that shallow work. Then sow without stirring the soil again.

This one sounded simple to me, and it is, just about. Miller waters his greenhouse plants in the forenoon, not the evening, and opens the vents on sunny days so plants don't stay damp. Fungal diseases, he warns, "explode in stale, damp environments."

Current advice backs him up. Picture tomatoes watered at dusk, still wet at midnight. That's where early blight and gray mold (Botrytis cinerea) get going. Water the soil in the morning instead, space and stake plants for airflow, and stay out of wet rows. Greenhouses need open vents or a fan, and patio pots need elbow room.

For run-down soil, Miller says green manure crops really help, along with soil tests. Bare soil takes a beating from winter rain. A cover crop holds it with roots and shades out weeds, too. Turned in or left on top, it adds organic matter. Legumes like crimson clover and field peas also pull nitrogen from the air, with help from root bacteria.

This late in fall, I'd go with cereal rye. Oats and field peas want a late-summer start, and a cold winter usually finishes them off. Crimson clover, available from Outsidepride on Amazon, needs a few weeks of growth before hard frost – unless your winters are mild, that one's an early-fall job. In spring, cut the crop around flowering, before seed sets, then wait two to three weeks to plant.

Farmers in Miller's community save back their own soybean seed, which he says "helps that variety to somewhat adapt to your farm's soil type." You don't need a farm for it. Save seed from several of your healthiest, most productive open-pollinated plants, not one favorite, and do it again the year after, too. Little by little, your seed comes from plants that thrive in your garden.

Beans, peas, lettuce, and tomatoes are the easy ones, because their flowers mostly pollinate themselves. Squash, cucumbers, and corn need isolation or hand-pollination, since bees and wind can cross them with nearby varieties. I'd skip F1 hybrids, though, since their seed can come up quite different. Dry your seeds well, then store them somewhere cool in labeled kraft paper seed envelopes.

Much of Miller's letter covers certification forms, buffer strips, and ice houses. But tucked in between are gardening ideas that today's research still backs up. Next season, I'm taking a slower look at my weeds and tomato leaves. You might notice things you've been walking past for years.

With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.
