#7734. Declaratory Judgment + $275K in Attorney Fees in Settlement of N.H. "XX" Wristbands Case

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The Institute for Free Speech, which litigated the case, reports on the settlement agreement:

Take off the wristbands or leave. That was the message Bow school officials gave parents and a grandfather who were silently protesting in support of female-only sports by wearing pink "XX" wristbands at a girls' high school soccer game in 2024…. After more than two years of litigation …, the Bow School District has agreed to a judgment declaring that it violated the plaintiffs' rights by barring them from wearing the wristbands at the game. U.S…. The settlement also provides $275,000 in attorneys' fees and costs.

The judgment declares that the plaintiffs "have a First Amendment right to silently wear pink wristbands bearing the XX symbol on the sidelines, in the spectator's area, or in the parking lot of any Bow District sporting event." It binds the district and its Board of Education, and it remains in effect even if the district amends its policies….

The plaintiffs wore the wristbands, whose "XX" symbols reference female chromosome structure, to protest a policy permitting a biological male to compete on the opposing girls' team. School officials, accompanied by a police officer, confronted them. The referee halted play until one spectator removed his wristband, and school officials later issued trespass orders barring Fellers and Andy Foote from school grounds, preventing them from attending their children's games and other school activities for a time….

After the district court denied a preliminary injunction in April 2025, the plaintiffs appealed. In August 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit ruled in the plaintiffs' favor, finding that they "have established a likelihood of success as to their viewpoint discrimination claim." The court concluded that the protest "fell short of harassment and disruption," and that school officials "cannot favor one side of a debate involving parental speech on an issue of prominent public concern." …

Here's my August post excerpting the First Circuit's opinion, written by First Circuit Judge Sandra Lynch, joined by Judge Jeffrey Howard:

On September 17, 2024, [plaintiffs] were instructed by Bow High School officials to remove pink "XX" wristbands they wore in protest while watching their daughters (in [one plaintiff's] case, granddaughter) play in a girls' soccer game against a team with one transgender athlete. Further sanctions followed…. [W]e conclude that appellants have established a likelihood of success as to their viewpoint discrimination claim arising from the sanctions imposed on them for their passive speech in wearing these wristbands….

The district court analyzed the school playing fields and adjacent parking lot, as appellants requested, under the mode of First Amendment law applicable to limited public fora as to impermissible viewpoint discrimination…. [The] appellee school district argues that this case must be analyzed more in the mode of Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District (1969) … [and other cases that] recognize the particular interests inherent in the public elementary and high school settings, and the necessary discretion given to public school administrators in the difficult job of running public schools….

Neither of those two different classic modes of First Amendment analysis, urged on by these opposing parties, is a perfect fit for this public high school speech case, and we note that the Supreme Court has not addressed this precise question. We need not and do not reach the complex question of which (or whether) either of these alternate modes is the appropriate First Amendment type of analytical model for the facts of record here. We conclude that on these facts the differences in analysis would not affect the outcome here….

The school's legitimate interest in regulating certain kinds of speech on the playing field sidelines … is not demonstrated by the evidence in this record. There is no evidence that appellants' protest caused a material disruption [which would be relevant under Tinker]. There was no disruption until school officials chose to intervene, after which the referee suspended the game for approximately fifteen minutes and the school officials chose to impose restrictions on appellants' speech and impose sanctions. The appellants did not stage any pregame demonstrations; did not march, shout, chant, or otherwise disrupt the game; and did not confront Tirrell or any other player. Instead, they waited until halftime before donning the "XX" wristbands in a passive, silent gesture of protest. There is also no evidence of harassment, given there is no evidence in the record that any player actually saw the wristbands.

The lack of any evidence demonstrating harassment also defeats the school district's argument that it had an affirmative duty under Title IX to protect students from the speech in which appellants engaged…. While it is true that appellants chose to protest at the September 17 game because of Tirrell being a player, the record does not contain evidence of appellants engaging in harassment before or during the game. To the contrary, appellants did not shout, chant, make threats, or aggressively gesture at Tirrell to communicate their views against her participation. Nor is there evidence that Tirrell or any other player even saw the wristbands or "subjectively perceived the environment to be hostile or abusive."

Principal Fisk did note the challenges that transgender students face generally. But Fisk did not ever explain how appellants' display of the "XX" symbol constituted sufficiently severe or pervasive conduct to qualify as harassment under Title IX. And to the extent the district court concluded that the silent wearing of "XX" wristbands on the sidelines of a school soccer field, without more, always amounts to harassing speech, we disagree.

The school district responds that it may make "predictive judgment[s]" to proactively prohibit conduct that it believes will eventually lead to an actionable Title IX claim….. We agree with the general proposition. But the argument fails on the facts of this record…. We need not decide in this appeal whether and under what circumstances passive speech, on other facts, consisting of displaying the "XX" symbol on school property during school events could be reasonably thought to be harassing. But appellants' silent display of the "XX" symbol at the September 17 game fell short of harassment and disruption, and we conclude that the district court erred in holding that the school's interest in prevention of harassment justified the prohibition.

While it is a closer issue, we conclude that the school district likely was not justified in sanctioning the appellants for their passive speech based on its concerns derived from the earlier exchanges with the appellants and other parents. None of appellants' reported discussions, including their possible different methods of protest reported to Bow High School officials by other parents, led to any attempt to "heckle and intimidate" Tirrell. And that was evident both before and throughout the game.

It is true that Fellers initially attempted to convince his daughter to get the Bow High School players to wear the wristbands, but his daughter informed him that "she could not get full support from the team and was afraid that it would divide them." Fellers's Facebook post made the night before the game encouraged spectators "to protect the integrity and safety of female athletics" and "come out to support our XX Lady Falcons and show your solidarity with our girls' team." But the record shows only that the appellants and perhaps others of similar views engaged in a passive protest and only started the protest at halftime. While the school district may make predictive judgments about whether disruption may occur and "need not be certain of its forecast," it cannot use those projections to immediately suppress a passive, silent protest, that did not impair any of the legitimate school administration interests recognized by the Supreme Court.

This brings us to the school officials' other stated reasons for sanctioning appellants. Superintendent Kelley stated that the "XX" symbol conveyed an "exclusionary" message about gender. Principal Fisk, who ordered appellants to remove the wristbands, described the symbol both as "hateful" and as "anti-trans." As to these justifications for the sanctions imposed, the record evidence demonstrates the likelihood that the school district imposed sanctions on the appellants' wearing of the wristbands because it disagreed with the protest message conveyed….

Although the leading Supreme Court case on viewpoint discrimination in academic limited public fora, involved colleges and not high schools, and involved a limited public forum, both significant differences, Rosenberger's anguage about viewpoint discrimination is pertinent. "The government must abstain from regulating speech when the specific motivating ideology or the opinion or perspective of the speaker is the rationale for the restriction."

The characteristics of the school as a place of learning reinforce that administrators cannot favor one side of a debate involving parental speech on an issue of prominent public concern, and which, in those parents' views, concerned the safety of their children. As the Supreme Court stated in a case involving a high school football game, "learning how to tolerate diverse expressive activities has always been 'part of learning how to live in a pluralistic society.'"

Judge Julie Rikelman concurred in the judgment, reasoning that Tinker might not prohibit viewpoint-discriminatory speech restrictions, but that in this case the school district had accepted the viewpoint neutrality requirement:

The school district accepted that the limited public forum framework applied to the facts here and conceded repeatedly, both in its brief and at oral argument, that it could restrict speech at the September 17 soccer game only for viewpoint neutral reasons…. Although it did urge us to conduct our First Amendment analysis with the principles of Tinker in mind, it did so only in arguing that its actions were reasonable and thus satisfied the [reasonableness] prong of the limited public forum test….

With the school district's concession in mind, I agree that the record lacks evidence of actionable harassment or material disruption from the plaintiffs' speech at the September 17 soccer game. The record also demonstrates that school officials likely restricted the XX symbol because they viewed it as "exclusionary" and demeaning to transgender students. That amounts to viewpoint discrimination under relevant precedent.

Del Kolde, Brett Nolan, and Nathan Ristuccia (Institute for Free Speech) and Richard Lehmann (Lehmann Major List, PLLC) represent plaintiffs. were on brief, for appellants.

#7733. Maryland Man Convicted of $18.7 Million Medicare Fraud for Respiratory Testing Scheme Targeting Nursing Homes

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

A federal jury in the District of Maryland convicted a laboratory owner yesterday for taking advantage of nursing homes that needed COVID-19 tests during the pandemic and fraudulently billing Medicare more than $18 million for other expensive respiratory tests that nursing home residents did not need, physicians did not order, and, in many cases, were never performed.

“Mr. Britton-Harr’s decision to exploit elderly nursing‑home residents and inexperienced interns for personal gain during a global pandemic is unconscionable. This verdict reinforces our message: there is nowhere to hide for those who commit fraud. We will find you and prosecute you to the fullest extent of the law,” said U.S. Attorney Kelly O. Hayes for the District of Maryland. “The U.S. Attorney’s Office, along with our law-enforcement partners, remains committed to rooting out fraud and holding accountable those who exploit our vulnerable victims and who steal our taxpayer money.”

“This verdict sends a clear message: the FBI will aggressively pursue anyone who steals from American taxpayers,” said FBI Baltimore Special Agent in Charge Jimmy Paul. “Patrick Britton-Harr will now face the consequences of his greed and brazen crimes. In addition to this healthcare fraud scheme, Britton-Harr was previously convicted for investment fraud in which the FBI uncovered a separate scheme where he defrauded private citizens. The FBI and our law enforcement partners will not rest until fraudsters like Mr. Britton Harr are brought to justice.”

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Patrick Britton-Harr, 42, of Annapolis, offered COVID-19 tests to nursing homes across the country in 2020 when these facilities were desperate for COVID-19 testing services. After specimens were collected from nursing home residents and other laboratories performed COVID-19 testing, Britton-Harr billed Medicare for separate, high-priced respiratory pathogen panel (RPP) tests purportedly conducted in a laboratory he owned in Arizona. Britton-Harr falsely claimed to Medicare that treating physicians ordered these extensive RPP tests, which screened for more than 30 respiratory pathogens. In reality, physicians never ordered the tests for their nursing home patients, and several physicians testified at trial they had never ordered an RPP test for any patient during the entirety of their medical careers.

Through his company, Provista Health, Britton-Harr fraudulently billed Medicare $18.7 million for RPP testing purportedly performed in just six months, of which Medicare paid more than $7.2 million. Evidence at trial demonstrated how Britton-Harr exploited inexperienced employees, including a family member and high school and college aged interns, by directing them to bill Medicare for an RPP test every time a COVID-19 test was performed. Britton-Harr further directed the billing of RPP tests supposedly performed at his Arizona laboratory after he had already closed the laboratory, barred staff from working in the laboratory, and no longer had the equipment necessary to run RPP tests. Additional evidence at trial proved that Britton-Harr billed Medicare for RPP tests that were never performed, including billing for tests for nursing home residents who were already deceased.

Britton-Harr used the proceeds of his fraud scheme to fund a lavish lifestyle, purchasing, among other things, a $112,500 Porsche 911, and making $25,000 monthly mortgage payments on his Annapolis waterfront mansion.

The jury convicted Britton-Harr of five counts of health care fraud and one count of transactional money laundering. Britton-Harr faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison for each count. A sentencing hearing will be scheduled at a later date. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors.

Trial Attorney Chris Wenger of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Ari Evans for the District of Maryland are prosecuting the case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.

#7732. 13 Potted Plants You Can—and Should—Winter Indoors

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 9, 2026 5:31 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Plenty of gardeners place their houseplants outdoors for the summer and enjoy them indoors the rest of the year. So why not try a similar strategy, and save a little money while you’re at it, by bringing your favorite cold-tender plants inside when the temperature drops so they’ll be ready to grow again when spring and summer rolls around?

Before you bring your outdoor plants in for the winter, you’ll need to do a bit of preparation. Start by inspecting them for pests and treating, if necessary. Repot if a plant needs it, and cut down on (or eliminate) fertilizing. Some plants can simply be brought indoors as houseplants, others should be forced into dormancy for a few months of cool storage, and still others are best kept going by making rooted cuttings. The following are a few cold-tender plants that you can bring inside each winter and then continue to enjoy outside for many summers to come.

While some palm trees are hardy in the winters of the Deep South, most palms need help to survive winter temperatures, even only to 55 to 60 degrees Fahrenheit . It’s possible to cover and winterize some palms planted in the ground, but potted palms should come indoors (preferably to a bright, humid spot). Move palms to an indoor location that gets lots of light. Water them regularly to keep the soil moist until spring, and carry them back outdoors after nights warm back up to at least 50 or 60 degrees.

Leave cacti outdoors as late into the season as possible so that the combination of shorter days and cooler nights will stimulate a dormancy response. You’ll need to keep an eye on the thermometer and know the low-temperature threshold for your particular type of cactus. Some species may be able to withstand 20-degree temperatures, but others cannot. If unsure, move potted cacti indoors as soon as cold drops to about 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit.

Stop watering cacti 3 to 4 weeks before the move so the plants are dry, and check them carefully for pets like mealy bugs or mites. In general, cacti do best in a cool location with minimal water, as they go dormant. Transition them back outside in early spring, gradually introducing sunlight if the plants show any sign of burning.

Citrus trees can actively grow and flower in winter, and may also ripen fruit if they’re pollinated. Even without winter growth, it’s a good idea protect these plants during the chilly months. As the days get shorter, move potted citrus trees (typically, dwarf varieties of lime and lemon trees) to an interim space outdoors that gets some protection from the elements, like a porch with radiant heat, and cut back on watering.

Before the first frost, move the citrus tree into a brightly lit indoor room, ideally between 55 and 70 degrees Fahrenheit. Citrus plants are sensitive to the drying effects of air, so it’s best to position them away from heat vents and cold drafts. Provide supplemental humidity with a pebble tray or regular misting.

Move tropical hibiscus plants indoors when overnight temperatures reach the low 50s. Place them in a brightly lit room, and treat them like regular houseplants. Cut back on watering and fertilizing during these cooler months. Try to avoid heat vents and cold drafts, and put the plants on a pebble tray to boost the ambient humidity, if necessary. Prune tropical hibiscus three times during late fall and winter (October, December, and February) to maintain the plant’s shape.

Prune jasmine vines by at least 25 percent before bringing them in for winter, letting them adjust gradually by bringing them inside at night and slowly lengthening the time spent indoors. Some or all of the plant’s leaves will fall off, but new ones will grow again in time. Bring jasmine into a sunny room before frosty weather arrives, and keep it away from drying air vents and drafts. Use a pebble tray to boost humidity to about 30 percent.

Coleus plants are grown for their stunning foliage and adaptability to shade. The plants are annuals in most regions, though, since they do not like temperatures below 50 degrees Fahrenheit and cannot survive temperatures below freezing. Bring the potted plant indoors once nights hover near 50 degrees. Repot the plant if it is outgrowing its container.

Another option is to propagate coleus stems to use next spring. Cut a 6-inch healthy stem, remove low leaves, and dip the stem in a rooting hormone before planting it in a container with moist potting mix. Cover the container with a plastic bag for a few weeks and keep it in a warm and sunny spot; water regularly.

Aromatic rosemary is a favorite cooking herb for many fall and winter dishes. However, the plant does not always survive winters in USDA Zones 6 or lower. Start by planting a rosemary in a well-draining container. Bring potted rosemary indoors before the first freeze. Keep it in a cool location with fairly high humidity, but avoid overwatering; if its roots stay damp and cool, it can develop root rot.

Feel free to harvest from the plant, but never cut off more than about 20 percent of the foliage and avoid cutting into woody main stems. You also can propagate rosemary indoors at the end of the season with 4- to 6-inch cuttings from a stem with no flowers.

Elephant ears, or taro, is a tropical plant that can survive a light frost only; a true freeze will kill the tuber. Simply move potted elephant ears indoors to a cool bright location. For those grown in the ground, carefully dig up the elephant ear tuber when cool weather approaches and the foliage dies back (they won’t survive winter outdoors in USDA Zone 6 and lower). Cut stems down to about 4 to 6 inches, and gently wipe off excess dirt.

Place the tuber in a warm, dark location with good air circulation to dry out for a few days. Wrap the bulbs in paper or drop them in a paper bag and store them in a cool, dry, dark place. Check them periodically for rot (throw rotten ones away) and insect damage (treat with an insecticide). Beware that nearly all its parts are toxic to pets and people if ingested—we don’t recommend bringing it indoors if you have young children.

It is technically possible to bring Boston ferns indoors and overwinter them in their active state, but it gets very messy very quickly. Instead, let them rest. Put them in a cool, moderately light to dark location that will not freeze, like an unheated basement or garage.

Before bringing your fern inside, hose it down on a warm (60-degree Fahrenheit) day to spray away insects and loose leaves. Give it a light trim, and shake and ruffle the fronds to drop debris before carrying the plant to its indoor spot. Moisten dry soil as needed until spring. Don’t be alarmed if some leaves pale or drop.

Geranium is another plant that likes to sleep the winter away. Dig the plants out of the ground before the first freeze, and gently knock the soil off the roots. Allow the plants to dry in a cool, shady location for a couple of days. Place the plants upside down in a paper bag and close the top. Store them in a cool, dark location that stays between 55 and 60 degrees.

About 2 months before the last frost date, trim the stored geraniums and plant them in moist potting soil with two leaf nodes below the soil line. You also can propagate cuttings or bring potted geraniums indoors to a sunny window.

Thyme is a flavorful and aromatic perennial herb, but a tender one in regions 5 or lower. Plant culinary thyme in a container in spring, keeping it in a sunny, bright location with well-draining soil. Bring it indoors for winter before the first frost. If the herb’s roots are peeking though the bottom of the pot or it looks crowded, repot the thyme when you bring it in. It also can be divided easily.

Be sure to place the container near a sunny window with a western or southern exposure in a room that maintains a 60- to 70-degrees Fahrenheit temperature for most of the day. Prune or pinch off flowers to preserve the herb’s flavor. Water as needed, allowing the container dry out between watering. You can fertilize every week or two with a diluted solution of fish emulsion or liquid seaweed. Harvest sprigs as needed for winter dishes.

Although Musa basjoo, Musella lasiocarpa, and a few other banana trees are quite cold hardy, most will not tolerate extended freezing temperatures. Potted banana plants can be brought indoors to a bright, sunny room to spend the winter in a slowed active state. They can take up some space indoors, so you also can help them sleep through winter. As the weather cools, gradually reduce watering. Before the first frost, cut the plant to 6 inches in height and move it to a dark, cool location. Keep the soil just moist until the weather warms in the spring.

The stunning evergreen cordyline is hardy only in the warmest growing zones, but potted cordylines can be moved indoors when temperatures dip into the 60s. Place them in a spot with good ventilation and consistent indoor temperatures; avoid placing them near air vents or in drafty areas. Increase humidity around cordyline by situating it in a humid room or on a saucer filled with pebbles and water, and avoid fluoride-treated tap water. Although the plant does not require dormancy in winter, it does like a rest, so cut water some during fall and winter.

We’ll help you set up your first garden—whether that’s a few pots on your patio, a raised bed, or an in-ground plot out back—and select the right plants for your soil and region.

#7731. I Thought Multi-Tools Were a Gimmick — Then I Took One on a Camping Trip

If, like me, you think multi-tools are gimmicky gadgets, you might change your mind once you discover how handy they are when your toolbox isn’t within reach.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

I admit I scoffed when my partner first started raving about his Leatherman Wave+ multi-tool. I thought it looked like an expensive, over-elaborate gadget that was destined to gather dust in a junk drawer.

However, as a keen hiker and camper, I’ve discovered how useful it is to have pliers, knives, a saw, scissors, files and other tools packed into one compact, quality piece of kit. I’ve also watched my tech-obsessed partner regularly reach for its precision tools when tinkering with his electrical equipment.

Ahead, I’ll share how a tool I once dismissed as a gimmick earned a permanent spot in my pack, and what two experts think makes a Leatherman worth the price tag.

I had to realize that our Leatherman Wave+ isn’t meant to replace a well-stocked toolbox to understand its value. Instead, it fills the gap when dedicated tools aren’t conveniently available or really needed.

At home, I regularly use the tool’s tiny scissors to carefully prune dead leaves from our many houseplants, the knife to open packages and the small screwdriver to tighten the legs on my glasses. My partner is an IT professional who also has an impressive collection of synthesizers, and he regularly reaches for the tool to make small technical repairs and splice wires.

I’ve found the Wave+ even more useful when we’re borrowing my parents’ campervan, hiking, or camping. The bottle opener is handy for those after-adventure beers, the serrated knife slices baguettes for trailside sandwiches, the saw cuts small, dry branches for kindling, and the screwdriver has adjusted our portable stove and tightened folding chairs.

The pocket-sized multi-tool packs 18 functions into a stainless-steel form that measures just four inches when closed and weighs 8.5 ounces. Alongside the tools I’ve mentioned, it has pliers, bit drivers, a wire stripper and crimper, a ruler, an extra knife blade and file, and an admittedly slightly-tricky-to-use can opener.

While I don’t regularly use all 18 tools, and I might never use some, having the selection provides peace of mind, especially in remote places.

Daniel Kilburn, founder of Emergency Action Planning and a preparedness expert, has carried his Leatherman Surge since his military service in 2006. “It’s an expedient tool to have on hand when you know you’re going to be someplace where you won’t have access to any others,” he says.

Scott Emanuel of knives, multi-tools, and outdoor equipment retailer Heinnie Haynes is also a multi-tool convert. He appreciated having one for quick fixes while renovating his cottage, and particularly rates the needle-nose pliers, which rival standard models rather than acting as an emergency substitute.

Kilburn suggests multi-tools can be a useful starting point for someone who doesn’t own a toolbox, and at the other end of the spectrum are the tinkerers and prepared problem-solvers Emanuel sees as natural fits.

“The person who will value a Leatherman is the one who spends their after-hours in the garage building stuff that they probably never need, it’s the kind of self-reliant and prepared person who you rely on to solve a problem,” Emanuel says.

The Leatherman Wave+ currently costs $129.95, meaning it should be a well-considered purchase rather than an impulse buy.

It’s reassuring to know that you’ll be investing in a refined product designed because of a genuine practical need. Founder Tim Leatherman conceived a pliers-based multi-tool after encountering car and plumbing problems while traveling through Europe in the 1970s, and after careful development, he launched the original Pocket Survival Tool in 1983.

Today you’re paying for that established reputation and durable construction, and Leatherman backs its products with a 25-year warranty.

“They’re ridiculously well built, really well regarded, and their choice of tools is good,” Emanuel says. He describes sought-after Leathermans as the “collectible top end of the multi-tool market.”

Kilburn recalls seeing lower-priced multi-tools failing his comrades during their military career. “Some disintegrate over time because they were just cheaply made with poor-quality material [and] poor-quality steel,” he says. His Leatherman Surge, meanwhile, has lasted over 20 years. If replacing it again, he says he would choose Leatherman over his backup Gerber multi-tool because he prefers its feel and durability.

Leatherman makes a wide range of multi-tools, so it pays to consider which functions you’ll genuinely use. The Signal model adds outdoor-focused features suited to camping, including a ferrocerium rod, emergency whistle and sharpener, but omits scissors. I use scissors enough for plant pruning, first aid and gear repairs that the Wave+ remains the better fit for me.

If you’re unlikely to use most of its functions, a smaller, cheaper multi-tool could make more sense. The Wave+ is also heavier than minimalist models, and there’s a learning curve when figuring out where everything lives.

Don’t forget that a premium multi-tool only represents good value if you look after it. We remove dirt after outdoor adventures and dry and lubricate it before storing. We also avoid forcing it to tackle jobs better suited to full-size tools. I wouldn’t, for example, choose its compact saw over a dedicated full-size version for pruning substantial tree branches in my yard.

If you’re using a Wave+ in the UK, like me, be aware of the country’s knife laws. You need a “good reason” to carry it in public because its blades lock. However, Emanuel explains that the legal language is ambiguous, so you shouldn’t assume you can carry one wherever you go just because it’s part of a multi-tool.

The Wave+ has convinced me that a good multi-tool is more than merely an expensive gimmick. It may not replace dedicated tools, but having so many functions at my fingertips in a form that is so compact, portable and easy to use makes it a practical, worthwhile investment.

The Wave Plus is a multi-tool workhorse. It packs 18 tools in one, including sharp blades, spring scissors, wire cutters, and more.

#7729. 8 Reasons a Contractor Might Give You an Outrageously High Estimate

If you just got a quote for a home repair that made your eyes water, there's probably a reason it's so high. A team of contractors weighs in with possible explanations.

If you just got a quote from a contractor that was way more than you thought it would be, join the club…it happens to the best of us. In fact, it’s a pretty common occurrence. Sometimes, though, the quote is so high that you can feel your mouth forming words you shouldn’t be saying. As someone who has been on both sides of such interactions, I can say that contractors don’t like them any more than you do. They know you can shop around, and they need your business. So what’s the deal with ridiculously high quotes?

I didn’t find any shortage of contractors willing to weigh in on this topic — one that is near and dear to their professional hearts. If a quote just made you hyperventilate, take a deep breath and check out some of the possible reasons why it’s so much higher than you expected.

“If an HVAC unit has a defective part that needs replacement, most of my clients will immediately ask how much the replacement part costs,” says HVAC technician Tamer Sayed. “I always tell the current market price and the misunderstanding often starts here. A few clients forget to take into account the labor and consultation fees. They assume they only had to pay for the replacement part.”

The same thing can happen with plumbing and electrical jobs. The part needed to get things working again may be small and inexpensive, and it may only account for a small portion of the quote. Sometimes the labor quote seems excessive, and that’s usually because the client doesn’t understand what’s involved with the repair.

Jake Vincett, a builder from the UK, makes this observation: “A lot of the time, the customer is comparing quotes for different work, because the cheaper one has included a surface repair whereas the more expensive one has quoted for fixing the underlying problem…It’s common that the customer doesn’t know or consider the amount of work going into a project. A new driveway isn’t just laying tarmac – it’s digging out the old one, laying the sub base, etc.”

Plumbing, electrical and HVAC expert Bob Cardwell adds: “It’s often not only one problem to fix but a bunch of small fixes. Even though it might be possible to fix the original problem without addressing the additional issues, an experienced and reliable technician will not ignore them, will try to fix them and will discuss them with the homeowner.”

Failing to provide a quote that addresses underlying issues and then delivering a sky-high bill at the end doesn’t just make the customer unhappy, says HVAC and plumbing expert Ryan Osterkamp. “It can make them feel like we don’t know what we’re doing.”

Osterkamp is used to hearing customers say: “I can go get that part for $X at Home Depot.” What they aren’t thinking about is the amount of training and expertise that made it possible for our technician to quickly and accurately diagnose the issue, have the supplies they need in their truck and be able to do the repair same day. Sure, you may save money by going with the guy on Facebook that works out of an old, unlabeled truck, but if his work doesn’t hold up, will he fix it without giving you the runaround? Is he insured? Does he offer a warranty?”

Tariffs, inflation and the economy in general are pushing prices up, and the dollar has lost a lot of its purchasing power for the average American. The same is true for contractors. “The fact of the matter is, we’re working harder now and making less,” says remodeling contractor Kevin Cullen. “In today’s economy, a lot of people are chasing the price to the bottom and shopping for the cheapest number. Unfortunately, they usually get what they pay for.”

A contractor who knows problems might creep up, such as a rotten subfloor that needs replacement during a toilet repair, makes an effort to warn customers as part of the quote. Potential problems aren’t always obvious. “There are times,” says Nika Tveretinova, who operates an HVAC business in Sacramento, “when the actual fix isn’t that complicated, but it’s the access that makes things tough—especially with equipment installed in an attic or cramped quarters. Sometimes we also find an old installation that needs a safety or code correction before we can put everything back together.”

In such situations, a higher-than-expected quote that you can reject is far better than a higher-than-expected bill you have to pay because the work is already completed.

Joshua Kurz founded NumeralQ, a home improvement pricing guide, and he cautions against comparing a bid you receive from a contractor to information you find online. “Owners often find an estimate online, and rather than waiting for a bid, they assume that number will be the actual cost. These estimates are helpful when determining a budget, but they are not interchangeable for actual bids. A 1,500 sq ft roof in one market will not necessarily cost the same in another market, and bids can even differ for neighboring houses.”

If you find a guy on Facebook who charges a low price to do a repair, there’s no guarantee that the repair will last or be up to code. When that person makes a mistake, a licensed contractor working on the same system at a later date might have to fix it, especially when inspectors are involved.

“Over a 40-year career,” says Cullen, “I’ve found many surprises: unsupported headers, no king or jack studs, undersized headers, poorly installed headers that aren’t flush and have gaps, termite damage, carpenter ant damage, water damage, mold. That’s not every job, but you never know when a homeowner bought a house in which a Rube Goldberg did the work on it.”

Sometimes a house is in such poor condition that a small repair, such as stopping a plumbing leak, can turn into a major project that involves replacing pipes, walls or subfloors. Rather than simply declining the repair, some contractors will offer a ridiculously high quote to avoid falling into a sinkhole of extra work. If the customer accepts the quote, the contractor won’t lose money by taking the job. A customer who rejects a bid can keep shopping with no harm done.

#7726. Man's Criticism of Nonprofit Found to Be "Harassment," Leads to Order Banning Photographing Company's Directors and Officers

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Monday's decision in Lake Itasca Region Pioneer Farmers, Inc. v. Fenske, by Minnesota Court of Appeals Judge Bratvold, joined by Judges Ede and Schmidt:

Pioneer Farmers … is a Minnesota nonprofit corporation that "organizes and conducts annual public demonstrations of historical steam-powered agricultural equipment at Itasca State Park and elsewhere for educational and historical purposes." Pioneer Farmers also owns real property near the north entrance of Itasca State Park in Park Rapids. Appellant Gerald W. Fenske is a former member of Pioneer Farmers. Fenske's membership was revoked in May 2023 for, according to allegations by Pioneer Farmers, "repeated disruptive behavior and conflicts with other members."

In December 2025, Pioneer Farmers petitioned the district court for an HRO [harassment restraining order] against Fenske, alleging that Fenske engaged in harassment "directed at" Pioneer Farmers and its "directors and officers." Along with the petition, Pioneer Farmers filed an affidavit by its president, who averred that, following the revocation of his membership, Fenske made "false and/or misleading complaints to various Minnesota state agencies" about Pioneer Farmers. In response, Pioneer Farmers sent Fenske two cease-and-desist letters.

According to the president's affidavit, after receiving the cease-and-desist letters, Fenske contacted individual members, made "unfounded ownership claims regarding equipment" on Pioneer Farmers' property, and continued "to attempt to stir discord among associated organizations." Fenske also maintained a personal web page titled, "Itasca Pioneer Farmer's Show Cancelled—Allegations of Unsafe Boiler Operation Reason for Cancellation." The president averred that Pioneer Farmers had never cancelled its annual event "for that reason."

The HRO prohibited Fenske from contacting Pioneer Farmers directly or indirectly, including "taking pictures of a protected person without permission" of Pioneer Farmers. The HRO also prohibited Fenske "from being within 500 feet" of Pioneer Farmers' property. But the district court declined to prohibit Fenske from contacting Pioneer Farmers' "officers and directors," because Pioneer Farmers "failed to identify those individuals." …

If a district court finds reasonable grounds to believe the HRO respondent has engaged in harassment, it may issue an HRO that "orders the respondent to have no contact with another person." Fenske does not challenge the district court's finding that Fenske harassed Pioneer Farmers or the HRO's prohibition on Fenske having "direct or indirect contact" with Pioneer Farmers. {Fenske [also] does not challenge the HRO's reference to "a protected person," which is not defined in the HRO.} Fenske challenges only the HRO's prohibition against "taking pictures" of a protected person without the permission of Pioneer Farmers.

We understand Fenske to argue that photography is not direct or indirect contact under section 609.748, subdivision 5(a)(2)…. "The phrase 'no contact' is clear and understandable. The common meaning of the word 'contact' is a coming together or touching, as of objects or surfaces, the state or condition of touching or of immediate proximity, or connection or interaction; communication." In other words, the common understanding of "contact" includes immediate proximity, interaction, and communication.

Photography often involves immediate proximity to or interaction or communication with the subject of the photograph. Photography that involves any of these, therefore, is within the common meaning of "contact." Because the HRO statute authorizes the district court to prohibit Fenske from contacting Pioneer Farmers, and contact includes photography that involves immediate proximity to or interaction or communication with a protected person, the district court acted within its discretion by prohibiting Fenske from taking photographs of Pioneer Farmers. We modify the HRO to clarify that it prohibits photography that involves immediate proximity to or interaction or communication with a protected person without Pioneer Farmers' permission.

The court rejected a First Amendment challenge to the photography restriction. It concluded that the restriction was content-neutral:

It held that Fenske essentially waived any argument that the restriction fails the narrow tailoring required for content-neutral restrictions:

Fenske … maintains that Pioneer Farmers "made no showing at the evidentiary hearing that [his] photography, as opposed to other alleged conduct, constituted harassment." … When evaluating a content-neutral restriction as applied, appellate courts determine whether the restriction burdens "no more speech than necessary to serve a significant state interest" in light of "the specific circumstances presented by this case." … Because Fenske did not provide a hearing transcript, we cannot evaluate what arguments or evidence related to photography may have been presented at the evidentiary hearing; thus, we cannot examine "the specific circumstances presented by this case" to determine whether the HRO is narrowly tailored.

And it held that Fenske had likewise waived other objections:

In his reply brief, Fenske contends that the district court also violated the First Amendment by "prohibiting [him] from contacting board members, participating in governance, or speaking publicly about" Pioneer Farmers. Generally, issues not raised or argued in appellant's principal brief cannot be raised in a reply brief. Fenske's reply arguments extend beyond those raised in his principal brief; therefore, we decline to consider them.

For more on other, even broader, anti-harassment orders stemming from public criticism, see Overbroad Injunctions Against Speech (Especially in Libel and Harassment Cases).

#7725. How to Thaw the Frozen Housing Market

Today’s housing market is painful for just about everyone involved, from builders to buyers to sellers. Government failures over the last seven years froze the industry and made homeownership less affordable, but the problem could be solved if Congress would act. 

To understand the solution, though, we first must know how we got here.

Beginning in 2020, Congress increased annual spending by trillions of dollars, and the Federal Reserve simply created the money to cover the massive deficits. The Fed also pushed interest rates to near zero and bought mortgage-backed securities (MBS).

The low interest rates made it cheaper for the government to borrow, but also for everyone else to borrow, including would-be homebuyers. Lower mortgage rates allowed people to take on much larger mortgages without making monthly mortgage payments prohibitively expensive. The resulting bidding wars sent home prices to stratospheric levels.

Fed purchases of MBS were fuel on the fire. They incentivized banks to make more loans at lower interest rates, stimulating mortgage lending. That’s precisely why the Fed bought MBS for the first time in the wake of the mortgage meltdown in 2009—it was attempting to rescue the industry. This time, the Fed bought MBS from early 2020 through early 2022.

The result was even larger mortgages from even lower interest rates as home prices went to the moon. Additionally, the runaway spending, borrowing, and printing of money by the government devalued the dollar and sent inflation to 40-year highs. The weaker dollar also meant it took more of those dollars to buy the same home, further inflating prices, but it also caused the Fed to change course.

>>> Government Broke the Housing Market—Only This Will Fix It

What followed was the sharpest rise in interest rates in four decades. Suddenly, mortgage rates were three or four times their previous levels. Ordinarily, higher interest rates would put downward pressure on home prices so that monthly mortgage payments stay roughly the same, but that didn’t happen.

If you bought a home in 2020 with a 2 percent interest rate mortgage, you effectively can’t sell your home today, not without downsizing. If you sell today, your old mortgage gets paid off and your next mortgage will have an interest rate closer to 8 percent. You can’t borrow anywhere near as much on the next home, or your monthly mortgage payment will explode.

These golden handcuffs have kept many existing homes off the market and even those that are for sale have unrealistically high prices. Sellers want those high prices so they’ll have more money to put down on their next home and therefore need to borrow less. That makes the higher interest rate much less painful and keeps the monthly mortgage payment manageable.

But that’s left a massive mismatch between buyers and sellers. Would-be buyers can’t afford today’s high prices with today’s high interest rates. Homeownership affordability is near an all-time low because it takes 44% of the median household pre-tax income to afford a median-price home. The after-tax figure is well over 50 percent.

Consequently, pending sales of existing homes have fallen to the lowest level on record, a full one-third below the level from a quarter century ago.

>>> U.S. Government-Backed Homebuying Market Drives Up House Prices for Ordinary Americans  

The situation is painful for new homes too. Residential construction is trending down, and homebuilder sentiment has fallen to the lowest level in 14 years. Builders are being squeezed by costs 60% higher than before the pandemic, and buyers who can’t afford today’s prices. About two-thirds of builders are using sales incentives to clear inventory, with more than 40 percent cutting prices.

For transactions to increase and the housing market to clear, home prices ultimately need to come down relative to incomes, which will take time because sellers need to adjust their expectations. But lower interest rates would also give buyers some relief and reduce the lock-in effect on current homeowners looking to sell. 

That’s where Congress needs to act. The legislature has no direct control over interest rates, but they do control spending, which is at obscene levels. In the last fiscal year, which just ended on September 30, the federal government spent $7.4 trillion and had to borrow almost $2 trillion of it.

Everyone, including the government, competes for loans and that additional $2 trillion of competition drives up the price to borrow money, which is the interest rate. Reducing government spending would reduce the deficit and immediately put downward pressure on interest rates, including for mortgages.

Granted, other recent factors have contributed to higher interest rates—like the Iran war increasing oil prices, which increase inflation expectations, which increase interest rates. Ending that conflict would help stabilize energy markets and eventually reduce interest rates too. But it’s the spending that’s squarely within Congress’s control and which would have a faster impact.

But given the abundance of ineptitude and lack of fortitude within the halls of Congress, don’t expect those spending cuts anytime soon.

#7724. Blocking Data Centers at Home Could Put Americans’ Data at Risk Abroad

If artificial intelligence (AI) companies are boxed out of every jurisdiction in the United States, they may need to locate their infrastructure offshore instead. That may resolve not-in-my-backyard concerns and prevent utility rates from increasing—at least from data centers—but it presents other disadvantages that AI’s opponents are likely overlooking.

The most obvious is the economic loss caused by pushing out a booming industry. Another is losing autonomy over Americans’ data.

Why Offshore Data Centers Put Americans’ Data at Risk

Consider what happens to U.S. data that relies on infrastructure in countries that do not share our value of freedom of speech. Our data could be subject to the same censorship laws of our host nation.

Governments in countries in the Middle East control internet infrastructure and restrict connectivity by blocking encrypted services like WhatsApp, FaceTime, and Facebook Messenger. These governments also censor content that is anti-Islamic, critical of those governments, obscene, and offensive.

The region also faces political instability that could affect data center performance and reliability. Amazon Web Services recently announced that customer data stored in data centers in Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates was unrecoverable after drone attacks by Iran in March and April.

>>> Families and Students Need Guidance on AI

In another scenario, a host nation may place tariffs on data transmitted back to the United States or use our data as a bargaining chip. In March, the World Trade Organization’s multilateral moratorium on customs duties for electronic transmissions lapsed. The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement also prohibits tariffs on data transfers, but the future of this agreement is uncertain due to its ongoing review process and the recently renewed trade war between the United States and Canada.

Or say AI developers go to any of the European, South American, or East Asian countries that favor carbon emissions taxes or high fuel-use taxes. Like tariffs, taxes would be costs passed down to U.S. consumers.

These are some of the risks the United States faces if enough jurisdictions do not allow data center development domestically. Outside its boundaries, the United States loses control.

How AI Already Shapes Americans’ Daily Lives

Yet disillusionment with AI chatbots and disdain toward AI-generated content are growing. These objections are reasonable. People value human connection, critical thinking, and human multimedia rather than life-like imitations.

But rejection of AI is not as simple as abstaining from consumer-facing, general-purpose AI chatbots or objecting to AI-generated media. AI is embedded across systems in society, and regular people encounter uses of AI more than they realize.

For example, facial recognition technology or Face ID that allows users to unlock their phones, sign into password-protected accounts, and verify their age for age-restricted platforms with a quick scan of their face is enabled by AI software.

Prospective homeowners engage with home lending advisors who use AI-powered software to verify income and financial records and extract data from applications and other documents. AI can improve objectivity and efficiency of application reviews. Banks and credit-card companies use AI to analyze patterns and deviations in transactions for improved fraud detection.

Many physicians use AI to record and summarize clinical encounters. Modern medicine involves administrative tasks to maintain a medical history for patients, which helps inform patients and their providers. But these tasks are time-consuming and take away time providers can spend with patients. AI frees up some of providers’ time spent on administration.

Additionally, more physicians use the AI-powered medical search engine OpenEvidence to assist with complex diagnoses and research the latest treatment options. Modern medicine is advancing constantly; it is challenging even for specialists to remain informed of every new clinical trial, technique, or other development in their field. Unlike general-purpose AI tools, the platform complies with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and is trained not on the open internet but on peer-reviewed medical literature, which helps ensure its output is accurate and relevant. The tool is only made available to health care professionals with verified credentials.

Drivers relying on GPS navigation obtain real-time traffic information, alerts, and faster routes due to AI. AI analyzes historical and live traffic conditions to estimate arrival times, predict slowdowns, and determine routes.

So whether or not you embrace AI, you likely unknowingly use it or you are on the receiving end of its use. And each of these examples involves processing and collecting sensitive data that should be safeguarded.

Why the United States Needs Data Centers at Home

U.S. AI data sovereignty means Americans’ data captured by AI systems is processed and stored in the United States. It also means it is governed and protected by U.S. laws and regulations and not subject to the whims of foreign governments. Maintaining data sovereignty requires sufficient data infrastructure.

>>> What’s Really Behind the Call to Regulate AI

This is why it matters that we build AI data centers in the United States. Wishing for AI’s extinction will not yield the desired results, and neither will widespread moratoriums on data center developments.

But in this current environment where data centers are politically unpopular, the future of data sovereignty is at stake.

Ratepayers are right to be concerned with how potential data center developments may affect their utility bills and access to necessary resources. Homeowners and buyers are right to be concerned with how it impacts homeownership and quality of life.

AI companies and data center developers must be honest, transparent, and fair—generous, even—to escape their villain trajectory. State and local leaders have an opportunity to respond to their constituents’ concerns and make favorable deals—ones that raise revenue for their jurisdictions and ensure that ratepayers are not suffering. Moratoriums on development and excessive demands stall, if not kill, negotiations.

If data center developers have nowhere to go domestically, they will have to go abroad. It could have similar consequences on the U.S. economy as offshoring in other industries, and it would be a shame after all the efforts to reshore manufacturing and other supply chains. Most certainly, it would relinquish data sovereignty.

This piece originally appeared in The National Interest

#7723. Senator-Governor Klobuchar and the Problem of the Received Wisdom

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

[This post is co-authored with Professor Seth Barrett Tillman.]

On November 3, 2026, U.S. Senator Amy Klobuchar (Minnesota-Democratic Party) was elected Governor of Minnesota. It is expected that, at some point, she will resign her U.S. senate seat, then take up the governor's position, and subsequently make a temporary appointment to fill her then-vacant senate seat. That dance of musical chairs happens from time-to-time. But some have also reported that Klobuchar must resign her senate seat. CBS News quoted political science professor David Schultz (Hamline University, Minnesota): "At some point she's going to have to step down as U.S. [S]enator." That might be true pragmatically—as a matter of politics. And sometimes, federal and state constitutional and statutory law bar dual-officeholding. Sometimes, but not all the time. In these circumstances, the law does not expressly bar dual-officeholding where, as here, the two positions are U.S. Senator and Minnesota Governor.

The U.S. Constitution's Incompatibility Clause (Article I, Section 6, Clause 2) bars U.S. Senators and Representatives from concurrently holding certain other federal positions. The position of governor is a state, not a federal position. So, this provision has no application here.

The Minnesota State Constitution has a similar provision (Article IV, Section 5). That provision bars Minnesota's state (not U.S.) Senators and Representatives from holding other state and federal positions. Klobuchar is not a state Senator; rather, she is a U.S. Senator. So, this provision has no application here.

The federal double-dipping statute, 5 United States Code Section 5533 bars drawing two salaries for two positions, where both positions are at the federal level. It has no application to state positions, e.g., governor. Moreover, it does not bar actual dual-officeholding; rather, it bars receiving two streams of full-time compensation or salary. Again, this provision has no application here.

Beyond these express provisions of positive law relating to incompatible offices, there are two common law doctrines, announced by state and federal courts, relating to incompatible offices. The more narrow doctrine prohibits one person holding two positions where one position supervises the other position or determines its compensation. Here, the two positions—U.S. Senator and Minnesota Governor—neither supervise one another, nor determine one another's compensation. So, this doctrine has no application here.

Finally, there is a more expansive common law doctrine relating to incompatible offices. This doctrine holds that, where as a practical matter, one person cannot carry out both sets of duties connected to two positions, the two positions are incompatible. It might be argued that a governor, particularly in an emergency, must reside within her state, and that a U.S. Senator, should generally be on hand, at short notice, to carry out Senate business. Given the physical distance between Minnesota and Washington, D.C., it is not entirely frivolous to suggest that this doctrine might act as a bar here. But the bar here is not distance, it is whether one can practically carry out both sets of duties. Governors frequently leave their states for short periods of time—even for vacations. That's allowable as long as they are within reach by telephone or video link, and as long as they can return quickly in the event of an emergency. Likewise, the U.S. Senate can choose to accommodate a Senator with responsibilities distant from D.C.—the Senate could allow participation in debate by video link, and it could allow remote voting, as long as the votes are reasonably authenticated. In other words, it is not a slam dunk that this expansive doctrine should apply on these facts, particularly given that this doctrine is merely a judicial creation lacking any foundation in both the U.S. Constitution and the Minnesota Constitution. More generally, we should not allow ad hoc judicial creations to supersede democratic elections and add to the qualifications and incompatibilities expressly set out in positive law.

Having one person hold two government positions—including state governor and U.S. Senator—is not a particularly good result. But the fact that a result is bad does not mean, without more, that that result is barred by our law. Not every bad thing is illegal; not every bad result is unconstitutional. And pretending the U.S. Constitution and Minnesota Constitution bar what we think is bad today elevates our intuition into legal duties only by undermining what the legal system actually commands. And if today, our intuition is vindicated, we might do well to remember that tomorrow, it might be someone else's intuition being vindicated and in ways that we might come to regret.

Among those who have considered this issue, I expect that many (and, perhaps, most) believe, as Professor Shultz believes, that Klobuchar must resign her senate seat before she becomes Minnesota's governor. That is, of course, the received wisdom. And that should tell you all you need to know about . . . the received wisdom.

[Seth Barrett Tillman, Associate Professor. Maynooth University School of Law and Criminology, Ireland. Scoil an Dlí agus na Coireolaíochta Ollscoil Mhá Nuad.]

#7722. A World of Independent Nations

Introduction

It is a great pleasure to be here in Jerusalem, and it is especially fitting to discuss “A World of Independent Nations” here in Israel. If any nation understands the importance of sovereignty, national survival, secure borders, and the sometimes inconvenient necessity of putting its own people first, it is Israel.

I come here as an American conservative, as someone who has spent much of his career working on Europe, and I should probably confess at the outset, as an unreconstructed Euroskeptic. I realize that admitting you are a Euroskeptic at NatCon is not exactly an act of great personal courage. It is rather like announcing at Heritage that you have reservations about socialism or Islamism.

But I want to make a broader argument today.

National sovereignty and transatlantic cooperation are not opposites. They are not even in tension. Properly understood, national sovereignty is the basis for meaningful transatlantic cooperation.

For far too long, the foreign policy establishment on both sides of the Atlantic has presented us with a false choice. Either you believe in an ever more integrated West, governed by international institutions and supranational bureaucracies, or you retreat into isolationism. Either Brussels runs Europe, or Europe falls apart. Either Washington manages its allies, or America abandons them.

I reject that choice. There is another model. It is a world of sovereign nations that know who they are, control their own borders, govern themselves, defend themselves, and cooperate when their interests and values coincide—in other words, exactly the sort of international order conservatives should be trying to build.

The Nation-State Is Not the Problem

For the past several decades, nationalism has been treated in much of polite Western society almost as a pathology. Europe in particular was told that its terrible 20th-century history proved that the nation-state itself had failed.

The answer was integration. Then, more integration. Then, when integration produced problems, the answer was invariably still more integration. It reminds me a little of the old joke about socialism: The reason it has never worked is apparently because nobody has ever tried quite enough of it.

The European project originally presented itself as cooperation among sovereign countries. But over time, political authority moved steadily away from national governments and toward institutions increasingly removed from national electorates. As I argued in “U.S. First Principles vs. European Bureaucratic Overreach,” the European Union has increasingly transferred authority away from sovereign nations and into distant institutions with limited democratic accountability.[REF]

This matters because democracy requires a Demos. Someone has to be able to answer the simplest political question there is: Who governs? And if you dislike the answer: How do you get rid of them?

That is easy to understand in a nation-state. It becomes considerably less clear when authority is dispersed among commissioners, courts, councils, agencies, treaties, and qualified-majority voting. It is difficult enough getting rid of a bad congressman. Try voting out the European Commission.

Europe Is Not the European Union

This leads to a distinction that American policymakers repeatedly fail to make: Europe is not the European Union. Europe is a civilization. Europe is a collection of ancient nations. Europe is Britain and France, Poland and Hungary, Italy and Greece, the Baltic States and the Nordic countries, and many others, each with its own history, traditions, loyalties, interests, and democratic institutions. The European Union is an institution.

The two are not synonymous. In fact, one of the most damaging habits in American foreign policy has been to confuse support for Europe with support for European integration. An America First foreign policy should stop doing that.

As I argued recently after Iceland rejected renewed EU accession talks in “Iceland Puts the Freeze on Brussels’ ‘Ever Closer Union,’” Washington should deal with Europe as it actually exists: as a continent of nations. America benefits when democratic allies control their own resources and interests and cooperate voluntarily, including through NATO.[REF]

That is not anti-European. It is profoundly pro-European. It says that the Czech Republic belongs to the Czechs. Poland belongs to the Poles. Hungary belongs to the Hungarians. Britain belongs to the British. And the United States belongs to Americans.

Perhaps this is considered radical these days. I prefer to call it self-government.

America First Does Not Mean America Alone

This brings me to America First.

America First is sometimes caricatured, particularly in Europe, as a doctrine of withdrawal. I think that completely misunderstands it. America First does not mean America alone. It means that American foreign policy should advance American interests.

And we should expect our friends to do exactly the same thing for their countries. America does not want European governments that obediently ask Washington what to do. America wants strong allies. America wants European countries capable of securing their borders, growing their economies, and defending their territory. America wants European NATO members capable of bearing a much larger share of the burden of defending Europe. America wants allies, not dependencies.

That is why sovereignty actually strengthens transatlanticism. America does not ultimately form alliances with regulatory systems. It forms alliances with nations capable of making decisions and honoring commitments.

A weak country that has surrendered responsibility for vital decisions is not made stronger merely because it sits inside a larger bureaucracy. A self-confident nation that can defend itself, control its territory, and act politically is a much more useful ally.

Where Conservatives Must Cooperate

But this cannot mean conservatives retreating behind their own borders and ignoring one another. Quite the opposite: Each nation must decide questions of free speech, border control, family, faith, energy, economic freedom, and defense for itself—but those debates increasingly reach across the Atlantic.

We should be candid. President Trump’s style can sometimes unsettle even our European conservative friends who agree with him on borders, sovereignty, and burden-sharing. That is no reason to abandon cooperation. European conservatives need not become Trumpists. Friends can disagree over tactics, trade, Ukraine, or NATO and still work together where their interests and principles coincide.

So, what should cooperation look like? It should begin with permanent working relationships among think tanks, lawmakers, legal groups, and campaigners. It should be built around particular battles, not a single manifesto. We can cooperate on free speech without agreeing on every foreign policy question.

And it should connect sovereign actors directly: Congress with national parliaments, attorneys general with legal advocates, and governments with governments—not everything mediated through Brussels.

The agenda is clear: speech, borders, family, faith, energy, economic freedom, and defense.

The test is simple. Cooperation should make each nation more capable of governing itself, not less.

A Practical Framework: A Transatlantic Conservative Compact

I propose a Transatlantic Conservative Compact. Not a treaty. Not a bureaucracy. And certainly not a conservative Brussels.

It would be a voluntary network linking conservative governments, lawmakers, think tanks, and legal groups around specific projects. Small working groups could share model laws, legal briefs, and campaign lessons on speech, borders, family, energy, and defense. Members could join one project and decline another.

That is the model. Not uniformity: cooperation.

Free speech is the obvious place to begin because rules written in Brussels or London can govern American platforms and affect what American users see.

The EU’s Digital Services Act can fine the largest platforms according to global turnover.[REF] In 2024, EU Commissioner Thierry Breton even warned Elon Musk before his interview with Donald Trump—an American political event.[REF] Britain’s Online Safety Act can likewise reach services based abroad and impose enormous fines.[REF] Faced with that risk, platforms will often censor first and ask questions later.

American and European conservatives should expose these demands, challenge them in court, and defend clear legal protections for political and religious speech. Alliance Defending Freedom, among others, is doing stellar work in this area.

In “European Democracy Shield: A Threat to Free Speech and Democratic Accountability,” I argued that American and European conservatives need to work more closely together to protect freedom of speech and conscience.[REF]

Border control and mass migration are another such issue. Individual nations must decide whom they admit, who is entitled to remain, and what obligations newcomers owe to the society receiving them. That responsibility cannot simply be outsourced upward.

Borders are not an embarrassing leftover from an unenlightened past. They mark the territory within which democratic government operates. If a government cannot determine who enters its country or effectively enforce its immigration law, we should ask in what meaningful sense it remains sovereign.

Here, American and European conservatives have a great deal to learn from each other. The objective should not be identical policies imposed from above. It should be the exchange of ideas among sovereign governments pursuing the interests of their own citizens.

That also means confronting Islamification directly. Religious liberty must be protected, but political Islam and parallel societies must not be tolerated. Newcomers who wish to live in Western nations must accept our laws, our civic order, and our civilizational inheritance. They need to integrate—or leave.

A Transatlantic Conservative Compact would also involve working together on issues like energy security, economic freedom, family policy, religious liberty, and the defense of Western civilization—and, of course, defense.

The transatlantic alliance remains important, but NATO should be an alliance of sovereign countries accepting reciprocal obligations, not a mechanism for permanently transferring responsibility for European security to the American taxpayer. If European nations are sovereign, then sovereignty comes with responsibilities. One of them is paying for your own defense.

I suspect even my European friends will concede that this particular American enthusiasm for national sovereignty is unlikely to disappear.

Europe Beyond the EU

At Heritage’s Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom, this is increasingly becoming a central part of our work.

Heritage is organizing a major event in Washington called “Europe Beyond the EU.” Its starting point is deliberately provocative: What if the future of Europe is not deeper integration? What if the real intellectual challenge is to imagine European cooperation after the age of centralization? In this tenth-anniversary year of the Brexit referendum, our December 8, 2026, conference will open that conversation, exploring what a European order rooted in sovereign nation-states might look like and how American conservatives can support it.

And we intend to go much further. Our planned Transatlantic Sovereignty Initiative will develop practical alternatives to centralized control over democracy, speech, trade, energy, economic policy, borders, and security. The purpose is not simply to criticize Brussels. It is to develop a positive conservative architecture for cooperation among self-governing nations.

That distinction matters. Euroskepticism cannot simply mean saying “No.” Eventually, we have to explain what we are saying “Yes” to. The answer is a flexible Europe.

  • NATO for collective defense.
  • Bilateral and multilateral agreements where they make sense.
  • Trade among free nations.
  • Voluntary arrangements on security and migration.
  • Cooperation without political absorption.
  • Partnership without permanent centralization.

I have called this elsewhere a functional Europe: sovereign nations using the institution appropriate to the task rather than assuming every problem requires transferring yet another power upward.[REF] That principle works beyond Europe as well.

Conservative Solidarity Without Conservative Globalism

There is, however, a trap here for our own movement. Conservatives rightly criticize globalism. We should therefore be rather careful not to invent a conservative globalism of our own. Our purpose cannot be to replace one transnational ideological establishment with another.

A Hungarian conservative will naturally put Hungary first. A Polish conservative should put Poland first. An Israeli conservative should—and most definitely does—put Israel first. And I make no apology for saying that an American conservative should put America first.

The miracle is not that our interests will always be identical. They won’t. The opportunity is that sovereign nations which possess civilizational confidence can nevertheless recognize enormous areas of common interest.

We can defend the freedom to speak.

We can defend religious liberty.

We can defend the family.

We can secure our borders.

We can resist unelected bureaucracies claiming powers voters never willingly surrendered.

We can defend the inheritance of Western civilization without demanding that every Western nation become politically identical.

And we can maintain a strong Atlantic alliance without asking either Americans or Europeans to surrender their independence.

That is my idea of transatlantic conservative solidarity. Not bland uniformity: solidarity. Not supranational government: cooperation. Not a homogenized West administered from Washington, Brussels, Davos, or anywhere else: a West of free nations.

Conclusion

For most of my professional life, the dominant assumption has been that history was moving relentlessly away from the nation-state. National loyalties were supposedly becoming obsolete. Borders would matter less. Supranational institutions would inevitably become stronger. Politics would become increasingly managerial. And ordinary voters would eventually learn to accept all of this.

I am increasingly convinced that precisely the opposite is happening. The nation has returned because it never really went away.

People want government close enough to control. They want borders that mean something. They want political leaders who are accountable to them. They want to preserve what makes their country their country. And they are increasingly impatient with institutions that tell them these desires are somehow illegitimate.

This is not a crisis for democracy. It is democracy reasserting itself. The challenge for conservatives is to turn that democratic revolt into a durable political order.

A world of independent nations need not be a world of isolation. It can be a world of vigorous cooperation precisely because that cooperation is voluntary.

A confident America should want confident allies. A sovereign Europe can be a better American partner than an increasingly centralized European Union. And nations secure in their own identity are better able to cooperate because they do not fear that cooperation requires their disappearance.

So my argument today is ultimately very simple: Sovereignty is not the enemy of Western unity. It is the foundation of it.

The future of transatlanticism should not be ever closer union. It should be ever stronger nations: independent, democratic, self-confident, able to disagree, able to cooperate, able to defend themselves, and willing, when our principles and interests align, to stand together.

That is the transatlantic alliance worth defending, and that is a world of independent nations worth building.

Paul McCarthy is Senior Research Fellow for European Affairs in the Margaret Thatcher Center for Freedom at The Heritage Foundation. This lecture is adapted from remarks delivered at NatCon Jerusalem on October 8, 2026.
